articles.full_text:
Britain will deploy Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom against increasing attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels, the UK government announced on Tuesday.
The aircraft will protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure from drones and missiles, the Ministry of Defense said. They will not carry out offensive strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen.
"The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable," British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said.
He particularly condemned attacks on Riyadh's international airport, which has been targeted 20 times since the beginning of October.
Strikes on the airport have killed at least 18 people and wounded hundreds this month, according to reports.
What additional military support is Britain providing?
The deployment follows a request from Saudi Arabia and expands military assistance announced by London in September.
Britain will also send an Atlas A400M military transport aircraft and military advisers. It has extended its offer to provide air-to-air refueling for Saudi aircraft operating against the Houthis for another 90 days.
The announcement comes as Yemen's civil war continues to escalate following the collapse of a years-long truce in September.
Houthi attacks have increasingly targeted Saudi oil facilities and civilian infrastructure. The rebels have also imposed a naval blockade and attacked tankers, disrupting oil exports and pushing up energy prices.
Inside Yemen, authorities said a Houthi strike on Monday killed 58 people at a training camp for Saudi-backed government security forces.
Saudi Arabia and the United States accuse Iran of supporting the Houthis, an allegation Tehran denies.
How is the conflict affecting Saudi Arabia's economy?
Saudi Arabia has postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference, informally known as "Davos in the Desert," until 2027.
The event, originally scheduled for October 26-29, was expected to attract leading international financiers.
According to media reports, major banks and private equity firms had raised security concerns about attending the event.
The conference is a key part of Saudi Arabia's efforts to attract foreign investment and diversify its economy away from oil.

articles.title: Iran's Ghalibaf meets Khamenei amid US-Israel tensions
articles.summary: Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf held talks with Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei on the latest military and economic developments involving the United...
articles.full_text:
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf held talks with Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei on the latest military and economic developments involving the United States and Israel, as well as information warfare, Fars News Agency reported Wednesday.
The meeting focused on strengthening Iran’s national capabilities, maintaining social cohesion and national unity, and improving cooperation between the government and parliament to address economic and livelihood challenges.
The two also emphasized advancing relations with Iran’s strategic partners, the same source said.
Ghalibaf briefed Khamenei on parliamentary activities since the outbreak of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran on Feb. 28 and outlined ongoing and future plans to address the country’s challenges.
The meeting marks another rare reported encounter involving Khamenei, who has not made a public appearance since succeeding his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in March.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian earlier said he had met Khamenei twice since he assumed office in March, including a meeting in August that lasted more than seven hours.
Khamenei was selected as Iran’s supreme leader on March 8, following the death of his father in U.S.-Israeli strikes on Feb. 28.
Since assuming leadership, Khamenei has communicated primarily through written statements, while his absence from public view has fueled speculation about his condition and role in the country’s decision-making.
The latest meeting comes amid continuing tensions between Tehran and Washington over security arrangements in the Strait of Hormuz and their broader conflict.

articles.title: Yemen’s Houthis declare peace talks with Saudi Arabia deadlocked, threaten wider escalation - Business Upturn
articles.summary: Yemen’s Houthis declare peace talks with Saudi Arabia deadlocked, threaten wider escalation  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
Yemen’s Houthi movement has declared negotiations with Saudi Arabia at a dead end, accusing Riyadh of attempting to impose its demands on the Yemeni population and warning that it is preparing for a broader escalation of the conflict. The statement, attributed to the group’s leadership in Sana’a, comes amid renewed fighting and rising tensions between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis have argued that Saudi Arabia has failed to advance previously discussed proposals and address restrictions affecting Yemen’s ports and airports. The group says it will not accept conditions it considers unfair. The latest warning raises concerns about the future of diplomatic efforts to contain the conflict, although the statement alone does not confirm that a new military offensive has begun.
Dispute over negotiations deepens
Mohammed Abdulsalam, the Houthis’ chief negotiator and spokesperson, said in remarks reported by the Yemen Press Agency on October 18 that Sana’a had maintained direct and indirect communication with the Saudi side. He accused Riyadh of failing to take meaningful steps towards implementing previously discussed commitments and said the group had submitted several proposals.
Abdulsalam also called for restrictions on Yemen’s ports and airports to be lifted and humanitarian issues to be addressed under the proposed roadmap. These demands remain central to the disagreement between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia has rejected Houthi accusations that it is deliberately besieging Yemen. In a statement published by the Saudi Press Agency in July, the kingdom said northern Yemeni ports had received more than 300 ships carrying food, fuel and other goods during the first half of 2026. Riyadh maintains that restrictions are necessary to prevent weapons smuggling and comply with international measures.
Risk of renewed regional conflict
The latest warning comes as the conflict has intensified beyond the negotiating table. Recent reports describe Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and retaliatory military operations, raising concerns that the confrontation could spread further across the region.
The Houthis control Sana’a and substantial parts of northern Yemen, while Yemen’s internationally recognised government is based in the south. Saudi Arabia intervened militarily in Yemen in 2015 in support of the internationally recognised government.
A United Nations-brokered truce that began in April 2022 substantially reduced cross-border violence, although it formally expired in October that year. Subsequent diplomatic efforts have sought to establish a broader settlement, including arrangements for salaries, transport links, economic recovery and a nationwide ceasefire.
The UN has continued to urge the parties to pursue an inclusive political process, warning that renewed fighting would deepen Yemen’s humanitarian crisis.
What happens next?
The immediate concern is whether the Houthis’ escalation warning will translate into additional attacks or whether diplomatic channels can be reopened. Saudi Arabia and the UN have yet to announce a new agreement addressing the latest demands.
Any renewed military campaign could threaten regional security, disrupt shipping and worsen conditions for civilians in Yemen. For now, the group’s declaration signals a serious setback for negotiations, but the extent of any further escalation remains uncertain.

articles.title: Trump's push for Israel-Saudi relations faces obstacles amid elections, Houthi attacks - analysis - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: Trump's push for Israel-Saudi relations faces obstacles amid elections, Houthi attacks - analysis  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump’s renewed call for Saudi Arabia to accept Israeli assistance against Yemen’s Houthis has revived questions about whether shared security threats could bring Riyadh and Jerusalem closer to normalization. But mounting attacks on Saudi infrastructure, Israel’s approaching election, and unresolved disagreements over Palestinian statehood continue to complicate the prospect of formal relations.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Asked on October 16 whether Saudi Arabia should accept Israeli help, Trump replied: “I do, I think they will. Israel’s been very helpful to Saudi Arabia.” He also suggested that Saudi-Israeli normalization could be back on the table, “maybe more than ever.”
His comments did not establish whether Riyadh had requested Israeli military assistance or agreed to any overt security partnership.
Saudi Arabia is confronting an intensified campaign by the Iran-backed Houthis, whose missiles and drones have targeted airports, oil facilities, and shipping. An attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed 13 people, while repeated strikes have disrupted aviation and raised concerns about the kingdom’s ability to protect infrastructure central to its economic development plans.
For Riyadh, however, accepting Israeli military assistance would carry political consequences at home and throughout an Arab region deeply affected by the wars since October 7, 2023.
“Since the Yemen war, there have been contacts with Israel. Israel wanted to assist with the Houthis, but the Saudis, because of public opinion, did not guarantee any open contact,” Dr. Yoel Guzansky, senior researcher and head of the Gulf Program at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), told The Media Line.
A September 30 incident illustrated the limits of cooperation. Following the emergency landing in Saudi Arabia of a flydubai aircraft bound for Israel after an attack in its cockpit, Riyadh refused an Israeli request to allow military aircraft to retrieve the Israeli passengers, according to Reuters. The passengers instead returned on another flydubai plane.
“Saudi Arabia did the minimum and didn’t want any normalization,” Guzansky said, referring to the refusal to permit Israeli aircraft to land.
Before the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, Saudi Arabia and Israel had been moving toward a possible US-brokered normalization agreement. The subsequent wars and destruction in Gaza have made formal recognition considerably more contentious.
Riyadh has maintained that any agreement must include a credible pathway toward an independent Palestinian state, a condition Israel’s current government has resisted.
“Since October 7, the Arab world is very much against Israel. The Palestinian issue is formally at the center because it helps maintain a form of stability for Arab governments,” Guzansky said.
He argued that public opposition to Israel would remain a substantial obstacle even if the two governments identified additional areas of cooperation.
“There is no common ground between Israel and Saudi Arabia in terms of societies. Public opinion is against Israel in Saudi Arabia, and it will be hard to shift that.”
Saudi crown prince politically challenged by ongoing security crisis
For Dr. Cyril Widdershoven, senior advisor at Blue Water Strategy, the security crisis also presents an economic and political challenge for Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 development program depends heavily on foreign investment, infrastructure expansion, and the kingdom’s reputation as a stable destination for international business. Continued attacks on airports, ports, and energy facilities threaten those ambitions while increasing defense and reconstruction costs.
Widdershoven warned that mounting expenses and persistent insecurity could fuel domestic criticism of the crown prince, making an openly acknowledged relationship with Israel even more politically sensitive.
The economic consequences of the conflict are already apparent. On October 19, organizers announced that Saudi Arabia’s flagship Future Investment Initiative conference, originally scheduled for October 26–29, would be postponed until 2027. The decision followed deadly Houthi attacks and growing security concerns, although organizers did not explicitly cite the attacks as the reason.
Military considerations present another obstacle. Saudi Arabia has fought the Houthis for more than a decade, yet repeated air campaigns have failed to eliminate the group’s ability to strike across the border or threaten shipping through the Red Sea.
“I don’t think that Saudi is militarily able to crush the Houthis. Hurt them, yes. But to go inside Yemen is something else,” Widdershoven said. “I would say it’s like a potential Afghanistan or Vietnam scenario.”
He also warned that direct Israeli military involvement could expand the confrontation by provoking responses from Iran and allied armed groups elsewhere in the region.
“I would say to the Israelis, I would offer my help, but I would keep my soldiers out. Let’s have the Arabs deal with the Arabs.”
Saudi Arabia is meanwhile seeking assistance from regional partners whose involvement may be more politically acceptable.
On October 18, Egypt’s National Defense Council, chaired by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, agreed to support Saudi Arabia in defending itself against Houthi attacks. The Saudi defense minister also met the president of the United Arab Emirates as the two governments sought closer coordination despite longstanding differences over Yemen.
Turkey submitted the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan to its parliament for ratification on October 20.
Signed in August, the three-country pact provides for mutual defense if a signatory comes under armed attack. Turkish officials have indicated that assistance to Riyadh could include military equipment and intelligence sharing, while any Turkish troop deployment abroad would require parliamentary approval.
Britain also announced Tuesday that Royal Air Force Typhoon jets would conduct defensive patrols over Saudi territory, expanding British military support against Houthi missile and drone attacks.
“The Saudis need the Emiratis now in terms of Yemen. It is temporary, not fixing their competition,” Guzansky said, distinguishing immediate security needs from the continuing rivalry between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi.
Widdershoven similarly identified Egypt and the Emirates as potential partners while questioning how far arrangements involving Turkey and Pakistan would translate into operational commitments.
He also distinguished official diplomatic relations from informal contacts, suggesting that Saudi and Israeli representatives might continue discussions without public acknowledgment.
“So to expect that officially there will be a discussion between Riyadh and Jerusalem, I think that will not happen officially,” he said.
Change in Israel leadership could improve potential Saudi relations
Israel’s October 27 election adds another layer of uncertainty.
The vote, the first national election since the October 7 attacks, will determine whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu can assemble another governing coalition or whether opposition parties can form an alternative government.
Guzansky believes a leadership change could improve prospects for renewed contact with Riyadh.
“The elections are crucial in this situation, since a new government, the current opposition, would help a lot in terms of rapprochement,” he said.
Netanyahu, Guzansky added, “is not well seen in the Arab world.”
Widdershoven offered a similar assessment, suggesting that Saudi opposition to closer relations with Israel is tied partly to Netanyahu personally.
“I don’t expect that as long as Bibi Netanyahu is in power, that this will happen,” he said. “The current feeling in Saudi is not that they are anti-Israeli. I think that they are anti-Bibi Netanyahu.”
Yet a change of government would not necessarily remove Riyadh’s principal diplomatic condition.
Gadi Eisenkot, a prominent opposition contender, has avoided endorsing a two-state formula, while other parties seeking to replace Netanyahu hold substantially different positions on Palestinian statehood, settlements, and negotiations.
An opposition coalition united around replacing the prime minister would therefore not automatically agree on a policy capable of satisfying Saudi demands.
Washington faces its own political pressures ahead of the November 3 congressional midterm elections.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll published October 20 placed Trump’s approval rating at 31%, the lowest of either of his presidential terms, as Americans expressed growing frustration over high gasoline prices and the economic consequences of the war with Iran.
Trump endorsed Netanyahu’s reelection campaign on October 18, even as both experts interviewed by The Media Line suggested that a different Israeli government might be better positioned to improve relations with Saudi Arabia.
The endorsement highlights a potential conflict between Washington’s immediate political alliances and its longer-term ambition to expand the Abraham Accords.
“Trump may keep pushing rhetorically for normalization with Saudi, but in practice it is very different,” Guzansky said.
Iran extending US negotiations to deny Trump pre-midterm success
The approaching US elections are also influencing calculations in Tehran. Senior Iranian officials told Reuters that Iran had deliberately prolonged negotiations with Washington partly to deny Trump a political success before the midterms.
Widdershoven argued that Iran could continue pressuring its adversaries through threats to shipping, rising insurance premiums, and regional instability without necessarily launching another major military offensive.

articles.title: US orders embassy staff, families to leave Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: The U.S. State Department on Wednesday ordered non-emergency government personnel and their families to leave Saudi Arabia amid escalating Houthi attacks, while rejecting reports t...
articles.full_text:
The U.S. State Department on Wednesday ordered non-emergency government personnel and their families to leave Saudi Arabia amid escalating Houthi attacks, while rejecting reports that similar evacuation measures were being prepared across the Gulf region.
State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott dismissed earlier reports citing U.S. officials that Washington was preparing to withdraw diplomatic personnel and their families from embassies throughout the Gulf.
"This is inaccurate," Pigott wrote on social media platform X.
"The US Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only," he clarified.
Pigott said the decision followed attacks by Yemen's Houthi group against Saudi Arabia, including strikes targeting civilian airports and critical infrastructure that caused casualties and significant travel disruptions.
The clarification came after three U.S. officials said Washington was preparing to order departures from diplomatic missions across the Gulf amid concerns over a possible resumption of regional hostilities.
The U.S. Embassy in Riyadh issued a security alert on Wednesday about possible further attacks by the Houthis on Saudi Arabia, after recent deadly strikes, including on Riyadh's airport.
Pigott stressed that protecting American diplomatic personnel and their families remained the State Department's highest priority.
The move was due to a possible resumption of hostilities, particularly with Iran-aligned Houthi militia in Yemen, two of the U.S. officials said.
Two of the U.S. officials said the ordered departures would potentially involve the evacuation of all personnel and their families from the U.S. Mission to Saudi Arabia.

Dozens of Israeli Air Force fighter jets conducted a sortie on Monday, flying as far as the Iranian border, according to Israeli and U.S. officials.
Why it matters: The operation, more than 800 miles away from Israel, took place a week before the Israeli elections and on the same day Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at Israel's Ovda Air Base. The sortie wasn't connected to Hegseth's visit.
While some Israeli and U.S. officials said the sortie wasn't unusual and that it was meant to deter Iran, it could have led to a miscalculation, triggering an Iranian response andreigniting the war.
Behind the scenes: The exercise involved dozens of fighter jets and refueling aircraft, the sources said.
It followed a flight path consistent with a potential strike against Iran, passing through Syrian and Iraqi airspace.
As the aircraft approached the Iranian border, they turned around and returned to Israel, the sources said.
The intrigue: U.S. officials said the Israelis knew that Iran's air defense systems would detect the sortie.
According to the sources, Israel notified the U.S. in advance and described the operation as a training exercise intended for "power projection" and aimed at deterring Iran from launching attacks against Israel ahead of the elections.
However, some U.S. sources said they had the impression that Israel was hoping the Iranians would fire at the aircraft, providing a justification for launching strikes against Iran.
Fox News reported on Tuesday that the Israeli Air Force conducted a drill towards Iran.
Driving the news: Last week, Axios reported that Netanyahu and President Trump discussed in early October the possibility of launching a major newoperation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections.
Netanyahu told Trump he was concerned about Israeli intelligence indicating Iran was taking troubling steps to reconstitute its nuclear program.
Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir told Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine at the time that restarting the war in that timeframe could cause the Israeli elections to be postponed, given that Iran would probably retaliate, the sources said.
Trump initially seemed to be inclined to resume attacks, but then grew hesitant and eventually decided against Netanyahu's proposal.
State of play: An Israeli official said Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir will not allow any unjustified military activity that could undermine the Oct. 27 elections.
What he's saying: On Wednesday Netanyahu said at a military graduation ceremony that Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei "has decided to follow in his father's footsteps" and allowed Iranian scientists to move forward with building a nuclear weapon.
"He has taken the safety off, and Iran is once again trying to develop its bombs of death," Netanyahu said.
"Therefore, there is only one way to eliminate this threat once and for all: to overthrow the regime in Iran. And that is the directive I have given to the IDF, the Mossad and the security agencies," he added.

One killed, 8 injured in Dammam airport attack, Saudis say
An attack targeting the King Fahd International Airport in the eastern Saudi Arabian city of Dammam killed one person and injured eight others Wednesday evening, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said.
The authority said in a statement that injuries from the attack ranged from "minor to serious" and that material damage to the airport was also being assessed.
It did not describe what type of attack occurred, but the kingdom's airports have been targeted repeatedly by projectiles in recent days by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants.
U.S. troops reducing footprint at Middle East posts, sources say
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official told CBS News on Wednesday the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing regional threats from the Houthis and direct threats from Iran.
NBC News was first to report on the drawdowns.
Asked about the reports, U.S. Central Command spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins told CBS News: "We regularly move U.S. service members and assets to optimize mission readiness. We do not discuss related movements for operational security reasons. U.S. forces remain vigilant and ready to protect American personnel and interests across the region."
The U.S. State Department has also ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia, citing threats posed by the Iran-backed Houthis.
CBS News has learned several U.S. embassies in the Middle East have adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status.
The restricted operations status, which the department introduced in August amid flare-ups in the war with Iran, allows embassies to reduce staffing and services without fully suspending operations.
Debris from intercepted drone kills 2 in Saudi Arabia, energy ministry says
The Saudi energy ministry said that falling debris from the interception of a drone targeting an oil facility killed two people and injured two others on Wednesday.
"The attempted attack resulted in the deaths of two individuals, a Filipino and a Nepali, and injuries to two others," the ministry said in a statement. It did not say who launched the drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field near the UAE border.
State Department orders some U.S. government employees and family members to leave Saudi Arabia
The U.S. has ordered all non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as the kingdom faces escalating attacks by Houthi militants.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a social media post Wednesday.
The order came a few days after the U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and several other countries warned that hostilities could rapidly and without warning spread beyond areas already affected by the fighting.
"The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority, and we will continue to take all necessary steps to protect and support them," Pigott added.
U.S. will suffer "even greater strategic failure" if it chooses war over diplomacy, Iranian FM says
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi issued a warning to the U.S. on Wednesday afternoon, saying it should choose diplomacy over returning to war.
"Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust & reach a just solution," he wrote on X, sharing a link to an opinion piece in the Financial Times. "But if US chooses war over diplomacy, it'll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure."
Araghchi said earlier in the day that Iran and the U.S. were still involved in indirect negotiations via mediators over the seven-day ceasefire proposal from September. The proposal was outright rejected by President Trump, but Araghchi said the U.S. was trying to add further clauses to the agreement.
U.S. sanctions Greek law firm for alleged involvement in Iranian "shadow fleet"
The U.S. Treasury announced new sanctions on the Panamanian-Greek law firm Karnakis and Karnakis for involvement in Iran's "shadow fleet" as part of its Operation Economic Outcast.
The U.S. accuses Karnakis and Karnakis of being indirectly involved in Iran's illicit shipping operations for years. A "shadow fleet" refers to oil tankers that hide their true ownership in order to evade sanctions.
"Whether you are conducting illegal oil transfers at sea or sitting in the corner office of a law firm, if you are supporting the Iranian regime, we will find you and sanction you," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "Iran's facilitators must make a choice: Either you are with us or against us. We know who you are, we know what you're doing, and we will continue to take action."
The Treasury also said it sanctioned Singapore- and UAE-based shipping agents, including a fleet of cargo vessels that has directly taken part in Iran's "shadow fleet" and "helped generate substantial revenue for the Iranian regime."
Riyadh airport partially reopens after deadly Houthi strike
A limited number of Saudi airlines took off and landed at the country's main airport on Wednesday, two days after authorities notified airlines that they could resume operations with prior permission.
Saudia and FlyNas were operating flights Wednesday, according to flight-tracking data published by FlightAware. Major carriers, including Lufthansa and Air France, have canceled flights through mid-November.
Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has been hit multiple times this month by Yemen's Houthi rebels and shut down on Oct. 10. A strike two weeks ago killed 13 people and injured hundreds more.
The Houthis have acknowledged attacking the airport, claiming without evidence that Saudi Arabia provided military equipment to government forces through the facility.
Iran criticizes potential Egyptian involvement in Yemen war; Sisi promises only defensive actions
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said any interference in the Yemen war by Egypt or any other country would make the situation "more difficult."
"Egypt has sufficient experience to avoid entangling itself in such a highly complex conflict," said Iran's top diplomat in an interview with Iraqi state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya aired on Tuesday.
"We believe that any foreign presence or interference will only make resolving this issue more difficult," Araghchi noted.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Wednesday that Cairo's proposed military support for Riyadh was to "defend Saudi territory, and does not include an attack on Yemen," according to a statement from his office.
At a government event titled Egypt Forum 2026, Sisi said the "objective is to defend the kingdom's lands and borders, as well as those of any other Arab state, should it be requested of Egypt," his spokesman said in a statement.
Sisi on Saturday had asked parliament to authorize support for Saudi Arabia in its war with the Houthis, "if requested."
The parliament, which is stacked with supporters of the president, has since held two rare secret sessions, before postponing deliberations until next week.
Iran's new defense minister says first priority is meeting air force needs
Iran's newly appointed defense minister, Mehrdad Akhlaghi, said Wednesday his first hours in office were devoted to meeting the requirements of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Aerospace Force and the army's air defense units.
"We are not in a war of rhetoric in response to repeated threats; we are turning threats into greater readiness and more effective defensive power," he wrote in his first post on X since taking office.
Akhlaghi added Iran was concentrating on its objectives through the use of new technologies.
"We may eat dirt, but we will not give up our soil," he concluded.
Trump blocked Netanyahu's plan for multiday strikes on Iran, report says
President Trump blocked a planned Israeli multiday operation that would have resumed strikes against Iran on the weekend of Oct. 10, according to the Financial Times.

Yemen's Houthis claimed an attack on a Saudi target in Aden Wednesday, with smoke reportedly rising near the airport, marking the third strike in a week against the seat of the Riyadh-backed government.
"Our armed forces were able to target the Saudi enemy's operations room in the Badr camp in Aden with a ballistic missile," Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement.
A police official in Aden earlier said there had been a blast "caused by a Houthi missile," speaking on condition of anonymity for security reasons.
Two other security sources in the city told Agence France-Presse (AFP) the attack targeted a site near the airport that belonged to forces from the Saudi-led military coalition that has been battling the Houthis.
Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognized Yemeni government have recently come under sustained attack from the Iran-backed Houthis, shifting the focus of the wider Middle East war that erupted with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
Earlier Friday, two missiles landed within the perimeter of the airport, with the Houthis claiming the attack.
A day earlier, the Houthis launched a deadly missile attack on the presidential palace in Aden, hitting command centers located inside the al-Maashiq presidential compound, which is used by government forces and the Saudi-led coalition.
Al-Jumhuriya TV, meanwhile, reported renewed heavy clashes between Yemeni armed forces and Houthi fighters at the old airport and around Mount Han, west of Taiz city.
The developments come amid the internationally recognized government's ongoing military offensive against the Houthis in southwestern Yemen.
On Tuesday, the Yemeni army said it had carried out 744 attacks against the group over 24 hours, neutralizing around 200 of its members and destroying or damaging 90 vehicles and other military assets.
In July, a fragile 2022 truce fell apart after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa in defiance of Riyadh's control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
Later, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before seizing government-held territory in Yemen along the Red Sea coastline in a lightning campaign.
In response, the Saudi air force has been regularly targeting the Houthis in support of the Yemeni government.

articles.title: Macron secures Qatari LNG, Gulf diesel supplies amid French fuel price crisis - International - World - Ahram Online
articles.summary: Macron secures Qatari LNG, Gulf diesel supplies amid French fuel price crisis - International - World  Ahram Online
articles.full_text:
French President Emmanuel Macron said on Wednesday that he had secured additional liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies from Qatar during a three-day tour of the Gulf, as France seeks to strengthen its energy security and ease pressure from soaring fuel prices amid the war involving Iran.
“We secured during the winter period the equivalent of two terawatt-hours per month of LNG, which was important for us and which will allow us to move forward,” Macron told reporters in Doha, the final stop of his tour.
The commitments also include additional diesel supplies from Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), each of which agreed to provide an extra 100,000 tons a month. Together with additional volumes from Saudi Arabia, the commitments amount to around 295,000 tons a month, equivalent to slightly more than 10 percent of France’s usual diesel consumption.
The energy arrangements come amid growing public discontent in France over rising fuel prices. Authorities have introduced curfews following demonstrations over the cost of living that escalated into rioting and looting.
European diesel prices have climbed to nearly $200 a barrel amid the war involving Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, putting further pressure on households and businesses.
Earlier this month, the International Energy Agency urged member countries to accelerate pledged diesel releases and consider providing additional supplies as global markets tightened.
Qatar, one of the world’s leading LNG exporters, has extensive energy and investment ties with France. French energy company TotalEnergies is a partner in Qatar’s North Field East LNG expansion project, one of the world’s largest gas developments.
Macron met Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani at Lusail Palace on Tuesday. Their discussions covered bilateral relations and ways to expand cooperation, particularly in the economic, investment, security, and defence sectors, the state-run Qatar News Agency reported.
During the tour, Macron also called for the protection of freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global energy trade.
Macron also announced that France would organize a conference in the coming weeks to support the Lebanese Armed Forces, saying the pressure on Lebanon amid Israeli military operations in the south was untenable.
“I think it is useless to do it before the Israeli elections, but we will organise such a conference because it is unavoidable,” Macron told reporters in Doha.
Israel is set to go to the polls on Tuesday.
Macron said France and Qatar were ready to contribute to efforts to restore Lebanon’s sovereignty and stability and disarm Hezbollah. He stressed that these objectives required an Israeli withdrawal accompanied by confidence-building measures.
“Our objective is the sovereignty, the stability of Lebanon and the disarmament of Hezbollah,” Macron said.
The French president said the situation in southern Lebanon remained highly tense, with Israeli forces occupying territory south of the Litani River. He criticized the pressure on Beirut, saying that challenging Lebanon’s sovereignty was not the best way to address the issue of Hezbollah.
Progress on arrangements involving Hezbollah's disarmament, an Israeli withdrawal, and the deployment of the Lebanese army in the south has largely stalled.
Macron's Gulf tour also sought to deepen France's defence and investment partnerships with regional allies.
In Abu Dhabi, he met UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. The two countries exchanged a strategic defence partnership framework and signed agreements covering energy, artificial intelligence, and advanced technology.
Defence cooperation featured prominently in the UAE leg of the tour, with France and the UAE signing an intergovernmental agreement on cooperation on the Dassault Rafale F5 standard within their respective Rafale programmes.
Macron began his tour in Kuwait on Monday, where the two sides signed agreements, memorandums of understanding, and declarations of intent covering defence, civil aviation, artificial intelligence, investment, health, and academic cooperation.
The three-day tour combined efforts to secure energy supplies with closer defence, investment, and technology ties across the Gulf, against a backdrop of regional conflict and uncertainty over global energy markets.

articles.title: Red Sea and Bab el‑Mandeb Escalation Tightens Screw on Global Grain and Food Trade - CMB News
articles.summary: Red Sea and Bab el‑Mandeb Escalation Tightens Screw on Global Grain and Food Trade  CMB News
articles.full_text:
Renewed Houthi attacks around Bab el‑Mandeb disrupt Red Sea shipping, lifting freight and risk premiums for grains, oilseeds and sugar.
Renewed fighting around Yemen and the Bab el‑Mandeb Strait is tightening constraints on Red Sea shipping, driving up freight and war‑risk premiums for agricultural cargoes. While physical flows continue, traders report rising costs, longer routes and heightened operational risk for grains, oilseeds, sugar and containerized food products transiting this key chokepoint.
The latest escalation follows a series of missile and drone attacks by Yemen’s Houthi movement against Saudi‑backed forces and infrastructure, including deadly strikes on military camps and attacks near major airports. Regional powers such as Egypt and the United Kingdom have stepped up security support for Saudi Arabia, underscoring concerns that the conflict could spill further into Red Sea trade lanes near Bab el‑Mandeb, a narrow corridor already labeled as disrupted since late July 2026.
Headline
Red Sea Escalation Near Bab el‑Mandeb Raises Costs and Risks for Global Grain and Food Trade
Introduction
Fighting in Yemen has intensified in recent weeks, with Houthi forces carrying out some of the deadliest attacks in years against government‑aligned troops and expanding their presence along the Red Sea coast. These moves come on top of earlier operations aimed at projecting power near the Bab el‑Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most critical maritime chokepoints for energy and bulk commodities.
Although Yemeni government forces have recently claimed to recapture territory and resecure access around Bab el‑Mandeb, shipping conditions remain formally classified as disrupted, and insurers continue to treat the area as high risk. This keeps freight rates and war‑risk premiums elevated for vessels moving grains, oilseeds, sugar and other food products between the Black Sea, Middle East, East Africa and Asia via the Red Sea corridor.
Exclusive commodities on CMBroker
Immediate Market Impact
The direct impact so far is being felt through logistics and cost channels rather than outright supply losses. Disruption status at Bab el‑Mandeb since 20 July 2026 has forced shipowners and charterers to reassess routings, delay sailings, or demand higher freight to compensate for the heightened security risk.
War‑risk insurance premia for transiting the southern Red Sea have increased, particularly for vessels flying flags perceived as party to the wider regional tensions. In some cases, dry bulk and product tankers carrying wheat, corn, barley and sugar are seeking higher time‑charter equivalents, which feeds into landed costs for importers in the MENA region and East Africa. Traders report that some counterparties are looking at Cape‑of‑Good‑Hope diversions for sensitive cargoes, extending voyage times by 10–14 days and tightening tonnage availability. (Market feedback; directionally consistent with prior Red Sea crises.)
Supply Chain Disruptions
Operationally, the main risk is intermittent interruption of vessel flows through the narrow Bab el‑Mandeb passage if hostilities intensify or if missiles and drones target shipping lanes, as they have in previous Red Sea flare‑ups. Even without direct hits on merchant ships, near‑misses or military advisories can prompt temporary halts, convoying requirements or speed reductions.
Importers in the Horn of Africa, the Arabian Peninsula and the Red Sea littoral are among the most exposed, given their structural dependence on seaborne wheat and other staple imports. Any disruption risks amplifying local supply tightness just as many governments are rebuilding buffer stocks ahead of winter and Ramadan demand. For exporters in the Black Sea, EU and Americas, higher freight and insurance costs may narrow destination arbitrage and complicate sales into Red Sea‑adjacent markets.
Containerized food products, including dairy ingredients, edible oils and value‑added grocery items, also face higher costs and potential delays. Carriers may impose emergency risk surcharges on boxes moving via the Red Sea, similar to those seen during earlier waves of Houthi attacks on international shipping.
Commodities Potentially Affected
- Wheat and other grains: Key suppliers in the Black Sea, EU and North America rely on the Suez–Red Sea route to reach buyers in the Middle East, East Africa and South Asia. Higher freight and war‑risk costs can lift CIF prices and volatility for import tenders.
- Corn and feed grains: Poultry and livestock sectors in MENA and East Africa depend heavily on imported corn and barley; any shipping disruption could pressure local feed prices and margins.
- Oilseeds and vegetable oils: Flows of sunflower oil from the Black Sea and palm oil from Southeast Asia to Middle Eastern and Mediterranean markets commonly transit the Red Sea; delays or diversions may tighten prompt supply.
- Sugar: Raw and white sugar shipments crossing between Indian Ocean producers and Mediterranean refiners are exposed to routing changes and freight spikes.
- Containerized food and ingredients: Processed foods, dairy powders and food additives moving in reefer and dry containers via Suez may face schedule disruptions and surcharges.
Regional Trade Implications
Middle Eastern and North African importers are likely to bear the brunt of higher freight and insurance costs, as many rely on short‑haul shipments through Bab el‑Mandeb for bread‑wheat and other staples. Countries around the Horn of Africa, where food insecurity is already acute, are particularly vulnerable to even modest increases in landed prices and transit times.
In the near term, some demand may swing toward origins that can flexibly serve markets via alternative routes, including West African and Atlantic ports. However, replacing the Suez–Red Sea corridor at scale is costly and time‑consuming. Exporters with diversified logistics options—such as those able to route cargoes via both Atlantic and Indian Ocean basins—could gain a competitive edge in tenders where risk premia for Red Sea transit become prohibitive.
The escalation also interacts with existing Black Sea risks, where attacks on ports and shipping have already depressed Ukrainian and Russian grain flows and shifted more volumes onto the Danube and rail corridors. Combined, these choke‑point pressures increase the sensitivity of import‑dependent countries to any further logistics shock.
Market Outlook
In the short term, the market impact is likely to manifest through higher freight, elevated war‑risk premia and occasional spikes in futures prices whenever new attacks or shipping incidents are reported. Wheat and corn contracts are particularly prone to headline‑driven rallies given the concentration of demand along the Red Sea corridor and concurrent uncertainty in the Black Sea.
Traders will watch several indicators closely: any shift from targeted military sites toward direct attacks on merchant shipping; changes in insurance underwriting rules for Red Sea voyages; and signs that major importers are front‑loading purchases or diversifying origins. Further military involvement by regional and extra‑regional powers could either stabilize the corridor through enhanced protection or add to perceived risks, depending on how operations are conducted.
For now, base‑case expectations point to continued flows but at higher cost and risk, with periodic bouts of price volatility. If the conflict were to significantly disrupt traffic at Bab el‑Mandeb for a sustained period, a more structural re‑pricing of freight and FOB differentials into exposed destinations would be likely.
CMB Market Insight
The latest Red Sea and Bab el‑Mandeb escalation reinforces a broader structural theme: agricultural markets are increasingly shaped by geopolitical chokepoint risk, not just fundamentals in production and consumption. For risk managers, this argues for integrating route‑specific freight and insurance assumptions into pricing models, particularly for MENA and East African demand.
Procurement teams may wish to diversify both origins and logistics options where feasible, including alternative discharge ports and overland corridors, while monitoring basis movements between Atlantic and Indian Ocean routes. On the trading side, the combination of Red Sea and Black Sea tensions is likely to sustain an option value in nearby wheat and corn, making tactical hedging around geopolitical headlines an essential component of risk management in the months ahead.

Middle Eastern oil exports have returned to prewar levels as shipping companies use alternative routes to bypass chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz targeted in the conflict.
In the week to October 18, shipments from Gulf oil producers excluding Iran averaged 24.6mn barrels a day, higher than the 23.3mn prewar average, according to data compiled by Kpler.
That takes the seven-day average for exports to its highest level since mid-February, days before the US and Israel struck Iran, igniting a war that has stymied exports from the world’s biggest oil-producing region.
The figures, which are preliminary, are far more volatile than before the war. They include the Strait of Hormuz — through which the vast majority of the region’s prewar exports passed — as well as ship-to-ship transfers just beyond the narrow waterway and flows from Red Sea ports.
Shipments through Hormuz itself are still more than a third lower than before the war, the data shows.
Despite the rebound in the region’s exports, the oil price has been rising in recent months as markets for some oil products show increasing signs of strain, and on Tuesday Brent crude, the international benchmark, hit its highest level since May. On Wednesday it traded at $108.77 a barrel, flat on the day.
Saudi Arabia routed a lot of oil through its Red Sea port of Yanbu in response to attacks on ships sailing through the Gulf, but flows through this alternative route have dipped periodically in response to attacks on the pipeline that serves the port and on nearby ships. For instance, flows through Yanbu were lower following an attack in mid-September on the pipeline that connects Saudi oil production to the port. Those volumes have since rebounded after Saudi Aramco completed repair work on the pipeline.
Oil exports from the region have remained buoyant this month despite an uptick in attacks on vessels. UK Maritime Trade Operations, which monitors such incidents, has reported 28 attacks on shipping in the region in October, after 18 were recorded over September.
Two ships were targeted on Tuesday night, according to maritime security sources. One tanker was hit in the north of the Gulf near the Iraqi coast, showing the expansion of Iran’s attack range. The vessel was in the vicinity of Khor Al Zubair port, according to maritime security company Vanguard.
The second was struck in the early hours of the morning off the Omani coast, according to an alert from the Pakistani Navy.
Both of the crews were reported safe, despite a fire on board one, which was subsequently put out, maritime security company Vanguard said.

What to know about the Iran war today:

The latest attack targeted King Fahd International Airport in the eastern Saudi Arabian city of Dammam, killing at least one person and injuring eight others Wednesday evening, Saudi officials said.

- Despite global oil prices remaining near five-month highs, President Trump insisted Tuesday that "we're doing very well" with Iran, adding that he was yet to "make a final decision of which way do we want to win" the war, "the nice way or the not nice way."
One killed, 8 injured in Dammam airport attack, Saudis say
An attack targeting the King Fahd International Airport in the eastern Saudi Arabian city of Dammam killed one person and injured eight others Wednesday evening, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said.
The authority said in a statement that injuries from the attack ranged from "minor to serious" and that material damage to the airport was also being assessed.
It did not describe what type of attack occurred, but the kingdom's airports have been targeted repeatedly by projectiles in recent days by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants.
U.S. troops reducing footprint at Middle East posts, sources say
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official told CBS News on Wednesday the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing regional threats from the Houthis and direct threats from Iran.
NBC News was first to report on the drawdowns.
Asked about the reports, U.S. Central Command spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins told CBS News: "We regularly move U.S. service members and assets to optimize mission readiness. We do not discuss related movements for operational security reasons. U.S. forces remain vigilant and ready to protect American personnel and interests across the region."
The U.S. State Department has also ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia, citing threats posed by the Iran-backed Houthis.
CBS News has learned several U.S. embassies in the Middle East have adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status.
The restricted operations status, which the department introduced in August amid flare-ups in the war with Iran, allows embassies to reduce staffing and services without fully suspending operations.
Debris from intercepted drone kills 2 in Saudi Arabia, energy ministry says
The Saudi energy ministry said that falling debris from the interception of a drone targeting an oil facility killed two people and injured two others on Wednesday.
"The attempted attack resulted in the deaths of two individuals, a Filipino and a Nepali, and injuries to two others," the ministry said in a statement. It did not say who launched the drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field near the UAE border.
State Department orders some U.S. government employees and family members to leave Saudi Arabia
The U.S. has ordered all non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as the kingdom faces escalating attacks by Houthi militants.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a social media post Wednesday.
The order came a few days after the , Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and several other countries warned that hostilities could rapidly and without warning spread beyond areas already affected by the fighting.
"The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority, and we will continue to take all necessary steps to protect and support them," Pigott added.
U.S. will suffer "even greater strategic failure" if it chooses war over diplomacy, Iranian FM says
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi issued a warning to the U.S. on Wednesday afternoon, saying it should choose diplomacy over returning to war.
"Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust & reach a just solution," he wrote on X, sharing a link to an opinion piece in the Financial Times. "But if US chooses war over diplomacy, it'll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure."
Araghchi that Iran and the U.S. were still involved in indirect negotiations via mediators over the seven-day ceasefire proposal from September. The proposal was outright rejected by President Trump, but Araghchi said the U.S. was trying to add further clauses to the agreement.
U.S. sanctions Greek law firm for alleged involvement in Iranian "shadow fleet"
The U.S. Treasury announced new sanctions on the Panamanian-Greek law firm Karnakis and Karnakis for involvement in Iran's "shadow fleet" as part of its Operation Economic Outcast.
The U.S. accuses Karnakis and Karnakis of being indirectly involved in Iran's illicit shipping operations for years. A "shadow fleet" refers to oil tankers that hide their true ownership in order to evade sanctions.
"Whether you are conducting illegal oil transfers at sea or sitting in the corner office of a law firm, if you are supporting the Iranian regime, we will find you and sanction you," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "Iran's facilitators must make a choice: Either you are with us or against us. We know who you are, we know what you're doing, and we will continue to take action."
The Treasury also said it sanctioned Singapore- and UAE-based shipping agents, including a fleet of cargo vessels that has directly taken part in Iran's "shadow fleet" and "helped generate substantial revenue for the Iranian regime."
Riyadh airport partially reopens after deadly Houthi strike
A limited number of Saudi airlines took off and landed at the country's main airport on Wednesday, two days after authorities notified airlines that they could resume operations with prior permission.
Saudia and FlyNas were operating flights Wednesday, according to flight-tracking data published by FlightAware. Major carriers, including Lufthansa and Air France, have canceled flights through mid-November.
Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has been hit multiple times this month by Yemen's Houthi rebels and shut down on Oct. 10. A strike two weeks ago killed 13 people and injured hundreds more.
The Houthis have acknowledged attacking the airport, claiming without evidence that Saudi Arabia provided military equipment to government forces through the facility.
Iran criticizes potential Egyptian involvement in Yemen war; Sisi promises only defensive actions
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said any interference in the Yemen war by Egypt or any other country would make the situation "more difficult."
"Egypt has sufficient experience to avoid entangling itself in such a highly complex conflict," said Iran's top diplomat in an interview with Iraqi state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya aired on Tuesday.
"We believe that any foreign presence or interference will only make resolving this issue more difficult," Araghchi noted.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Wednesday that Cairo's proposed military support for Riyadh was to "defend Saudi territory, and does not include an attack on Yemen," according to a statement from his office.
At a government event titled Egypt Forum 2026, Sisi said the "objective is to defend the kingdom's lands and borders, as well as those of any other Arab state, should it be requested of Egypt," his spokesman said in a statement.
Sisi on Saturday had asked parliament to authorize support for Saudi Arabia in its war with the Houthis, "if requested."
The parliament, which is stacked with supporters of the president, has since held two rare secret sessions, before postponing deliberations until next week.
Iran's new defense minister says first priority is meeting air force needs
Iran's newly appointed defense minister, Mehrdad Akhlaghi, said Wednesday his first hours in office were devoted to meeting the requirements of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Aerospace Force and the army's air defense units.
"We are not in a war of rhetoric in response to repeated threats; we are turning threats into greater readiness and more effective defensive power," he wrote in his first post on X since taking office.
Akhlaghi added Iran was concentrating on its objectives through the use of new technologies.
"We may eat dirt, but we will not give up our soil," he concluded.
Trump blocked Netanyahu's plan for multiday strikes on Iran, report says
President Trump blocked a planned Israeli multiday operation that would have resumed strikes against Iran on the weekend of Oct. 10, according to the Financial Times.
The plan was designed to exceed the intensity of the joint U.S.-Israeli military offensive launched in February, three people familiar with the matter told the paper, and would have struck Iranian nuclear sites, regime targets and civilian infrastructure such as power plants.
The president blocked the strike to avoid escalating conflict before the U.S. midterm elections, according to the report.
Iranian regime needs to be toppled, Netanyahu says
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Wednesday he had directed the Israeli army and intelligence services to topple the Iranian regime.

JEDDAH: Saudi Arabia should develop a trade corridor through the Indian Ocean to reduce its dependence on the region’s two maritime chokepoints, Folk Maritime’s CEO said on Wednesday.
“We need, as a Kingdom, to be independent of either of the two straits. This is a lesson we have all learned,” Poul Hestbaek told the Saudi Maritime and Logistics Congress in Jeddah.
Speaking during the opening panel, “Fragmentation: Navigating the New Geopolitics,” he said: “How are we going to do it? Who is going to do it? I don’t know. This is way above my pay grade. But I think it is clear to everybody that we need to do this to feel protected in the future.”
His remarks highlighted the challenges facing shipping companies as they seek to maintain services, protect crews and secure supplies amid regional disruption.
Hestbaek described conditions in the Gulf as fragile. With traffic through the Strait of Hormuz back to about 75 percent of normal levels, he said, a single incident could reverse that recovery.
“It takes one missile hitting the right place, and they’re all gone. That’s how it works. It is so fragile, and to operate in that environment, you need a very agile organization.”
Crew safety comes before all other considerations, he said. When risks escalate, Folk Maritime makes participation voluntary, covers the costs of seafarers who choose to leave a vessel and offers them employment on other ships in its fleet.
“So, it is very clear that they are all on board because they want to be,” he said.
The company also increases external support, including intelligence, during periods of heightened risk.
As a company owned by the Public Investment Fund, Folk Maritime also prioritizes supply security for the Kingdom when making commercial decisions, Hestbaek said.
“The first and foremost requirement for getting on board our ships is: ‘Do you bring supply security to the Kingdom?’ That is number one.”
Insurance premiums in some trades had risen 24-fold within days, he said, with the additional costs passed on to customers. However, those costs remained secondary to crew safety, vessel safety and supply security.
Akshay Anand, group CEO of ABSA Al-Barrak Group, said that trade adapts to disruption rather than stops.
“Here in Saudi Arabia, we have been at the center of the Silk Road and trade routes for centuries. The essence of that arrangement is still the same. The modes have changed,” he said, pointing to cargo reaching the Kingdom from Turkiye through Syria.
Asked whether road freight could replace shipping, he said: “Can trucking replace ships? No. Very simply, no.”
Nevertheless, pressure on the wider transport industry was “massive,” he added.
“I, for one, am extremely proud of how we have endured the past couple of years. I think any other country in our situation would have buckled. We have remained strong. We have remained resilient.”
Speaking to Arab News after the panel, Anand said operators could no longer rely solely on established corridors.
“In the current scenario, you should not rely solely on traditional trade routes. You have fragmentation … when that happens, you have to find alternatives.”
The route through Syria was one of several options being used, he said, alongside other land routes, Saudi Arabia’s western ports and connections through Oman and the UAE.
Anand also called for greater cooperation in sharing the costs of disruption.
“I mean shared responsibility in the collective sense, rather than the legal sense: For cargo to flow effectively, everyone is responsible. It is not a case of one person’s responsibility beginning where another person’s ends.”
Costs “should not be imposed on the weakest party,” he added, calling for updates to legal frameworks, contractual terms and arbitration arrangements to support a more collaborative approach.
The panel also featured Essam M. Al-Ammari, deputy for maritime transport at the Transport General Authority. It was moderated by Valeria Ramundo Orlando, co-founder and managing partner of Equilibrium Climate Capital and GreenSquare Ventures.
A second session, “Competing for Cargo: What Shipping Lines Want and How Ports Win It,” examined what persuades shipping lines and cargo owners to commit business to a port.
Jay New, CEO of King Abdullah Port, identified three deciding factors: control, capabilities and connectivity.
Shipping lines increasingly seek ownership or operational control rather than relying entirely on independent terminals, he said.
“For a shipping line, relying on a third-party, independent port that it does not own carries an element of risk.”
Such partnerships increasingly involve commitments spanning “two, three or perhaps even more decades,” he added.
New said King Abdullah Port has 17 sq. km of land and capacity for 26 million twenty-foot equivalent units.
He also highlighted that disruption to regional shipping predates recent developments in the Gulf, pointing to pressure on Red Sea operations since late 2023.
“We think the disruption is all in the Strait of Hormuz, but this started a long time ago,” he said.
Over the past six to seven months, he had seen “substantial volume growth in the Red Sea, with cargo now coming into Saudi Arabia and moving across the Kingdom.”
That growth had prompted a review of connections between port stakeholders, including customs, the Border Guard, freight forwarders and inspection agencies.
Cargo owners may accept some delays, he said, but still need clear information about their shipments.
“Where is my container? Where is it? When will I get it?”
Efficiency depends on the performance of the entire chain, New added.
“You are only ever as efficient as your weakest link.”
Mohammed Badawy, chief operating officer of Folk Maritime Services, said liner and feeder operators assess cargo demand at both ends of a route, terminal reliability and the strength of partnerships before introducing a service.
“We need a terminal or port that understands our business and our needs, and is willing and able to work with us — not only when things are business as usual, but also when things go wrong.”
A delay of four to six hours can cause cargo to miss a connection and remain at a terminal for several days, he said.
“So communication, communication, communication — it is extremely important.”
Karim Omran, vice president, group commercial, at Red Sea Gateway Terminal, highlighted the continuing importance of price alongside connectivity and service quality.
Despite the wider advantages a port can offer, shipping lines often return to a direct commercial equation, he said, asking the question: “I don’t care about all this. How much discount can you give me?”
The session was moderated by technology journalist and broadcaster Lucy Hedges.
The day’s closing panel examined shipping fuels and the investment decisions facing operators ordering vessels that could still be trading in 2045, as the industry works toward net-zero emissions by 2050.
Yasser Towairgi, manager of the marine projects and engineering division at Aramco, highlighted the company’s experience using biofuels in its fleet, reporting carbon emissions reductions of up to 20 percent.
“The biofuel proved really good performance in terms of reducing carbon emissions, up to 20 percent reduction in carbon emissions, and it’s available locally,” he said.
Biofuels could be introduced without major investment in onboard propulsion systems, he added — a consideration for operators assessing alternative fuels that are not yet available at commercial scale.
Towairgi was joined by Samer Agha, industry manager at Zahid Tractor, which represents Caterpillar Power and Energy Systems. Ramundo Orlando moderated the discussion.
The congress also featured the signing of a professional partnership agreement between Bahri and the University of Jeddah. The organizations were represented by Hisham Al-Khaldi, Bahri’s chief support officer, and Noura Omair Al-Shahri, CEO of the Applied College.
The congress continues on Thursday with sessions on national logistics delivery, the offshore economy and maritime security, alongside a fireside discussion on the Red Sea’s coastal tourism potential and marine environmental protection.

articles.title: Qatari-French partnership: Growing investments, expanding horizons for economic cooperation - Qatar Tribune
articles.summary: Qatari-French partnership: Growing investments, expanding horizons for economic cooperation  Qatar Tribune
articles.full_text:
QNA
Doha
The economic partnership between Qatar and France extends well beyond trade volumes and mutual investments, embodying an expanding network of strategic interests that bridge capital with advanced industry, and French technical expertise with emerging Qatari market opportunities.
From a merchandise trade volume of approximately QR6.39 billion in 2025, to Qatar’s landmark commitment to invest EUR10 billion across key sectors of the French economy, including areas of mutual benefit, and with over 665 French companies operating in the Qatari market, the avenues for cooperation are diverse, offering expanding opportunities to transition toward a deeper and more integrated phase of partnership.
Amid global economic shifts, energy, artificial intelligence (AI), advanced technologies, infrastructure, and financial services stand out as key growth sectors driving diversification.
Data from the National Planning Council revealed that the volume of commodity trade between Qatar and France reached approximately QR6.39 billion in 2025. This consisted of QR2.44 billion in Qatari exports and QR3.95 billion in imports, resulting in a trade deficit of approximately QR1.50 billion. Qatari exports included QR1.51 billion worth of domestically produced goods, alongside QR937.9 million in re-exports. These figures reflect the scale of exchange, while highlighting the importance of broadening Qatar’s export base and enhancing the presence of locally produced goods within the French market.
Bilateral trade
According to the latest data for 2026, the volume of bilateral trade reached approximately QR1.32 billion, with Qatari exports valued at QR416.3 million and imports totalling QR904.9 million, underscoring the importance of developing the structure of trade exchanges, opening new avenues for exports, and maximizing economic opportunities.
Speaking to the Qatar News Agency (QNA), banking expert Abdullah Al Raisi emphasized that the economic ties between Qatar and France possess a strong foundation for transitioning towards an advanced phase of trade and investment cooperation driven by growing mutual interests and expanding opportunities in value-added industries that support Qatar National Vision 2030.
He noted that trade figures reflect the strength of this partnership, demonstrated by QR6.39 billion in trade exchange during 2025. This highlights the significance of the French market for Qatari companies, as well as the opportunities created by bilateral relations to expand trade and investment flows.
Looking ahead, he added, high-potential sectors for cooperation include advanced technology, artificial intelligence, clean energy, digital transformation, financial services, and tourism. Furthermore, there is significant potential to leverage French expertise in the development of infrastructure and strategic projects within Qatar.
Al Raisi noted that strengthening the partnership should go beyond increasing trade exchanges to attracting high-quality investments, establishing joint ventures, facilitating the transfer of knowledge and technology, and expanding private sector participation in both countries to generate sustainable economic value for both sides.
He further emphasized that the diversity of investment opportunities in Qatar, combined with French industrial and technological expertise, forms a solid foundation for building long-term partnerships capable of navigating global economic shifts and unlocking new horizons for growth and competitiveness.
665 French firms in Qatar
For his part, economist Dr Abdullah Al Khater told QNA that the Qatari-French partnership is long-term, diverse, and robust, citing the active presence of over 665 French firms in Qatar across key sectors from energy, led by TotalEnergies, to large-scale infrastructure.
Regarding Qatari investments in France, Al Khater explained that Qatar plays a vital role in France’s energy security through Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) deliveries to the Fos Cavaou terminal in southern France. He also noted that a Memorandum of Understanding between the Qatar Financial Centre (QFC) and the French Chamber of Commerce facilitates market entry for French firms expanding in Doha, a move that supports the Qatar National Vision 2030.
These data reflect the broad scope of economic relations between the two countries, as the French presence in the energy and infrastructure sectors complements the investment opportunities offered by Qatar, while the French market provides avenues for Qatari investments to enter strategic sectors and diversify investment portfolios.
Furthermore, the presence of French companies in Qatar paves the way for partnerships that extend beyond mere project execution to include the development of supply chains, the transfer of expertise, the enhancement of local capabilities, and the expansion of Qatari companies’ participation in projects with an international dimension.
Energy occupies a central position in this partnership, characterized by ongoing collaboration between Qatar and French firms operating in the sector, as well as the critical role of LNG in ensuring supply security and diversifying energy sources.
Key areas for cooperation
At the same time, advanced technology, artificial intelligence, digital transformation, and sophisticated industrial sectors have emerged as key areas for deepening economic cooperation, driven by a growing need for innovation, increased productivity, and the development of technical solutions across various industries.
The collaboration among financial institutions, chambers of commerce, and business communities serves as an additional avenue for expanding bilateral relations by supporting business growth and leveraging the competitive advantages present in both markets in alignment with long-term economic development priorities. This is achieved by facilitating market entry for companies, fostering communication between investors, and exploring opportunities for joint ventures.
Ultimately, commodity trade, investment volumes, and the corporate presence reveal a partnership with a broad foundation for growth, one that also offers scope for greater integration. Enhancing Qatari exports to France, attracting high-quality investments, expanding joint ventures, and linking commercial cooperation with the transfer of knowledge and technology are all pathways that can increase the economic returns from these bilateral relations. The objectives shared by Doha and Paris encompass the construction of a more diverse and sustainable partnership, providing productive ventures and long-term growth opportunities for both economies.

articles.title: Iran-Pakistan border trade halt leaves trucks and cargo stranded - Iran International
articles.summary: Iran-Pakistan border trade halt leaves trucks and cargo stranded  Iran International
articles.full_text:
Trade between Iran and Pakistan remained suspended at two major border crossings on Tuesday, leaving trucks and cargo stranded, with Pakistani authorities citing security and anti-smuggling measures and Iran pointing to technical difficulties.
Commercial traffic through the Gabd-Rimdan and Taftan crossings was halted as of October 20, although passenger movement reportedly continued at Gabd-Rimdan.
Pakistan described the suspension as a temporary measure to strengthen security and combat smuggling, while Iran attributed the disruption to technical issues and precautionary measures.
The two countries remain in contact to resolve the problem, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said on Tuesday.
The closures come as Iran increasingly relies on land routes to sustain foreign trade following restrictions on maritime shipping during the war.
Before the conflict and the US military blockade of Iran's southern ports, more than 80 percent of the country's foreign trade passed through the southern ports of Rajaei and Khomeini.
The diversion of shipments to road networks has increased transport costs and congestion, although land crossings lack the capacity to replace maritime trade.
Thousands of trucks stranded
Iranian media had already reported queues of approximately 3,000 trucks at Rimdan before the latest suspension, with some drivers waiting between 20 and 30 days to cross.
Limited processing capacity on the Pakistani side and requirements to transfer cargo from Iranian trucks to Pakistani vehicles have contributed to the delays.
An industry circular issued in August also described difficulties unloading Iranian trucks in Pakistan and transferring their cargo.
“I urge all truck drivers not to bring cargo toward the borders. The situation is so bad that since last night and throughout October 20, huge queues of trucks have been turning back. The border is closed and is being cleared. Do not come!” a person affected by the disruption told Iran International.
Another person contacted the broadcaster with a similar warning, urging drivers to avoid sending additional shipments until the crossings reopen.
The latest suspension has increased the risk of prolonged vehicle inactivity and financial losses for transport operators and cargo owners.
Talks continue on reopening
Negotiations with Pakistani authorities to remove obstacles at Rimdan were continuing, border market director Abdolsalim Hoot said on October 18, adding that perishable goods were receiving priority.
An official in Pakistan's Balochistan province also described progress in negotiations and the possibility of reopening the crossings soon.
No timetable for resuming commercial traffic had been announced by Tuesday.
Iran and Pakistan had previously set a target of increasing annual bilateral trade to $10 billion, but border disruptions, banking difficulties and limited freight capacity have complicated efforts to reach that goal.
The suspension also coincides with Washington's efforts to increase economic pressure on the Islamic Republic, including warnings of sanctions against countries and companies maintaining financial and commercial dealings with Iran.
