articles.title: Who are major candidates in Israel's upcoming general elections?
articles.summary: Israeli voters go to the polls Oct. 27 to decide whether to grant Benjamin Netanyahu another term or usher in a new political era. Polling shows a tight race between Netanyahu’s na...
articles.full_text:
Israeli voters go to the polls Oct. 27 to decide whether to grant Benjamin Netanyahu another term or usher in a new political era.
Polling shows a tight race between Netanyahu’s nationalist Likud party and his chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar! party.
Israelis vote for parties, which then form alliances to create a majority coalition. No single party has ever won a majority in the 120-member parliament, or Knesset.
Netanyahu, 77, is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister and the most dominant force in Israeli politics, having persevered through wars, crises and scandals. He is the longtime leader of the Likud party, and supporters point to his record on security and the economy, as well as his close ties with U.S. President Donald Trump, who has endorsed Netanyahu.
Netanyahu's opponents say he's responsible for the policy and security failures that preceded the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas incursion and accuse him of mismanaging the wars that followed. In 2024, the International Criminal Court issued a warrant for Netanyahu's arrest over allegations of war crimes and crimes against humanity. He is also embroiled in a yearslong legal scandal at home, having been charged with fraud, breach of trust and accepting bribes. Netanyahu denies any wrongdoing.
Eisenkot, 66, comes from a working-class family of Jewish Moroccan immigrants. He spent four decades rising through the ranks of Israel's military, eventually becoming the chief of staff. The general currently leads the largest opposition party – the centrist Yashar! – after entering politics in 2022. His son and two nephews were all killed in combat in Gaza following the Oct. 7 incursion.
Eisenkot also served as an observer in Netanyahu's war Cabinet, but resigned after eight months, when he accused the prime minister of lacking a clear strategy. He has since positioned himself as a moderate alternative to Netanyahu, but remains hawkish on security. Eisenkot is credited with formulating Israel’s so‑called "Dahiyeh Doctrine,” a military strategy calling for the use of disproportionate power in areas where attacks are launched.
If he succeeds in forming a coalition, Eisenkot could become the first Israeli prime minister of Mizrahi descent. Israel's Mizrahim, who come from North Africa and the Middle East, have historically faced discrimination from the country's European-descended elite.
Naftali Bennett, 54, is the right-wing and religiously observant leader of Beyachad (Together), a joint ticket with centrist politician Yair Lapid. He opposes Palestinian independence and supports settlement-building in the occupied West Bank.
Before entering the Knesset in 2013, Bennett served as Netanyahu's chief of staff and also was head of the Yesha Council, an umbrella organization of local authorities inside Israeli settlements. His conservative Yamina party won seven seats, which helped him cobble together a coalition of both left-wing and Arab parties. He then briefly served as prime minister in 2021, the result of a power-sharing agreement, also with Lapid.
While Bennett, like Netanyahu, takes a hard line toward the Palestinians, the two men have deep disagreements over Netanyahu's handling of security issues and his battle against the Israeli legal system.
Itamar Ben-Gvir, 50, is Israel's national security minister and a far-right provocateur with multiple convictions, including for supporting a terrorist organization. He leads Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power), an ultra-nationalist party whose strong showing in the last election secured him his Cabinet post and helped push Netanyahu's coalition further to the right.
He is a trained lawyer who gained recognition by successfully defending right-wing Jewish extremists accused of violence against Palestinians. When Ben-Gvir was a teenager, the military refused to draft him because of his extreme views. He was also a follower of Meir Kahane, the violently racist rabbi who advocated for expelling Palestinians from Israel, Gaza and the West Bank.
Ben-Gvir has also laid out plans for what he says would be the "voluntary" emigration of roughly 2 million Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, where he has advocated for re-building Jewish settlements.
Mansour Abbas, 52, is a Palestinian Arab politician and dentist from northern Israel. He leads Ra'am, the first Arab-led party to join a governing coalition in 2021.
His strategy has been to focus on more local issues, such as crime in Arab communities, rather than the larger Israeli-Palestinian conflict, in the hopes it will win Ra'am more seats in the Knesset and court potential coalition partners.
As part of this push, Abbas named former police commander and centrist Jewish politician Yoav Segalovitz as the number two candidate on Ra'am's electoral list. Abbas has served in the Knesset since 2019.

Saudi Arabia has not responded to inquiries regarding the execution of two Bangladeshi nationals, which was carried out without prior notification to Dhaka, Bangladesh’s Foreign Ministry said Wednesday.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said earlier this week that Dhaka has sought clarification on the circumstances of the executions, which were carried out on Oct. 14.
The government has asked for copies of the court verdicts, details about the offenses and an explanation of why Bangladesh's diplomatic mission was not informed, she added.
Saudi Arabia is Bangladesh's largest overseas labor market and home to an estimated 3.5 million Bangladeshi workers who send home major remittances, making migrant welfare a key bilateral issue.
The Saudi embassy in Dhaka did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Saudi Arabia's Interior Ministry said a man and a woman were executed after being convicted for committing "indecent acts" inside a mosque in the holy city of Mecca, Saudi media reported.
Islam said the government would decide on next steps after receiving the case details and documents and discussing the matter with Saudi authorities.

Russia’s Presidential Administration has ordered state and Kremlin-aligned media outlets to begin writing about “Putin strikes” on Ukraine, two employees at such outlets told Meduza.
The Presidential Administration’s political bloc sent loyalist media recommendations advising them to report that “the effectiveness and efficiency of Russia’s strikes far exceed what the Ukrainian military has achieved.”
“Our ballistic weapons have performed flawlessly. The Ukrainian regime has lost its most important production and storage sites, where cruise missiles and drones, along with their components, were assembled and stored. ‘Putin strikes’ are far larger in scale and more effective than enemy attacks. We are shutting down the militants’ missile programs, which helps keep Russia’s regions secure,” the guidance document says.
Headlines, comments from servicemen, and articles using the phrase “Putin strikes” indeed appeared this week in major Russian media outlets.
For example, the Russian news website Gazeta.ru published an article with the following subheadline:
“SVO” veteran Konovalov: “Putin strikes” deprive the Ukrainian military of the ability to fight.
The outlet cites Vitaly Konovalov, head of the Association of Veterans of the Russia-Ukraine War in Stavropol Krai, who says the strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure are allegedly aimed at undermining supplies to the Ukrainian military. Notably, Konovalov himself never uses the phrase “Putin strikes.” It appears in the connecting phrases and generalizations added by propagandists.
Novye Izvestia published an article titled “Putin Strikes on Ukraine: Ukrainian Military Left Without Electricity and Weapons.” Rosbalt used the phrase in the headline of a news item titled “Putin Strikes on Ukraine: Ukrainian Military Losing Logistics Hubs, Substations, and Vessels.” It also appears in headlines and articles from Fedpress. Segodnia.ru writes about a “series of “Putin strikes.”” The phrase has even appeared in pro-government Instagram accounts.
A political consultant who works with the Presidential Administration’s political bloc said directly linking Putin to the strikes on Ukraine is meant to try to boost the president’s approval ratings.
According to polls by the Public Opinion Foundation (FOM), Putin’s approval rating fell from 75% in July to 71% in early October, while trust in him fell from 74% to 70% over the same period.
“In this case, [the idea is to raise the ratings] among the pro-war, ultra-patriotic segment of society, who need to be shown some successes from the war. To the question “What has been accomplished?” [at the front], the suggested answer is “Putin strikes,” by analogy with the “Stalinist strikes,”” the consultant said.
During Joseph Stalin’s rule, the term “Ten Stalinist Strikes” referred to 10 major Soviet army operations during World War II.
The source told Meduza that it is hard to assess how effective the appearance of “Putin strikes” in the press has been: “Maybe it will have some effect on the older segment [of society].”
Speaking at a press conference in Bishkek on September 1, following the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit, Vladimir Putin said he had ordered the Russian military to prepare and carry out massive strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities. “They’re striking our people, so they’ll get a response,” he added.
In mid-October, discussing the Russian army’s strikes on Ukraine, Putin said:
They took the first step. We started responding. Now they’re whining about energy facilities too, and about other targets, including data centers and so on. They started it. They shouldn’t have started it.

Dallas is set to host Unicorn Rodeo, a Texas-style technology conference bringing together the state’s business community and leading Israeli startups and entrepreneurs. The event opens with an exclusive VIP dinner on October 20, followed by a full conference day on October 21 at the W Hotel Dallas.
Presented and produced by the Texas-Israel Alliance, the conference will connect Israeli entrepreneurs with Texas-based investors, corporate executives and policymakers to develop commercial relationships between the two markets.

As the world’s eighth-largest economy, Texas offers Israeli companies a significant platform for investment, strategic partnerships and access to the broader US market. The program will explore how Israeli innovation can connect with Texas’ business and industrial scale through investment, strategic partnerships and access to the US market.
At least 50 speakers will participate across 10+ sessions covering artificial intelligence, defense technology, cybersecurity, healthcare and biotechnology. An Israeli startup showcase will highlight emerging companies, while a live Q&A with US go-to-market experts will address the practical challenges of entering and expanding in the American market. Johnson; and Doug Deason, president of Deason Capital Services. ANKARA: Pakistan, Turkiye, Qatar, and Indonesia signed an agreement on Wednesday to boost defence cooperation and strengthen defensive capabilities, the Turkish Defence Ministry said.
In a statement, the ministry said the countries signed the “Badr Memorandum of Understanding” in Doha as a sign of their desire to further deepen cooperation and develop partnerships.
Badr (بدر) is an Arabic word meaning full moon (the bright, complete moon).
“The agreement holds substantial economic importance,” it said, adding the accord sought to foster cooperation in military production, boost military capabilities, and help collaboration in technical military training, research and development.
“By leveraging the unique military production capabilities of each country, the initiative will facilitate cooperation and integration, enhance defense industrial capacities, and enable the fulfillment of the needs of allied and friendly nations,” it added.
Turkiye, which has NATO’s second-largest army and a robust defence industry, has been helping Gulf nations, including Qatar, where it has a military base, bolster their defences.
In August, it signed a mutual defence pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, under which an attack on one party constitutes an attack on all. Ankara also has close ties with Indonesia, notably in the defence industry.
The ministry said the Badr accord would strengthen ties between the countries’ defence industries and bolster collaboration to promote security and achieve shared objectives.

The UAE positions itself at the heart of industrial transformation as supply chains evolve
The world’s manufacturing map is being redrawn, and the next generation of industrial powerhouses may look very different from those that dominated the previous century. Low-cost labour, vast factory complexes and access to cheap raw materials are no longer the only factors determining where products are made. Technology, supply chain resilience, energy security and proximity to emerging consumer markets are increasingly influencing industrial investment decisions.
For the UAE and the wider Middle East, this transformation presents a significant economic opportunity. A region traditionally associated with energy production, international trade and large-scale infrastructure development is increasingly positioning itself as a destination for advanced manufacturing.
From precision engineering and pharmaceutical production to aerospace components, electric mobility and industrial automation, the possibilities extend across multiple sectors. The ambition is not simply to manufacture more products locally, but to build sophisticated industrial ecosystems capable of competing internationally.
At the heart of this transformation is a fundamental change in how companies evaluate manufacturing competitiveness. Efficiency remains essential, but reliability, flexibility and technological capability are becoming equally important.
Globalisation created manufacturing networks that stretched across continents, allowing companies to source materials, components and finished products wherever costs were lowest. These arrangements delivered extraordinary efficiencies, but also exposed businesses to vulnerabilities when supply chains were disrupted.
Geopolitical tensions, shipping bottlenecks, changing trade policies and unexpected interruptions have prompted manufacturers to reconsider their dependence on concentrated production centres.
The result is a growing emphasis on diversification. Businesses are exploring regional manufacturing hubs, alternative sourcing arrangements and production facilities closer to important customer markets.
This does not necessarily signal the end of global manufacturing networks. Instead, it suggests a more distributed industrial landscape in which companies balance international sourcing with regional production capabilities.
The Middle East occupies an interesting position within this emerging geography. Located between major Asian manufacturing economies, European consumer markets and Africa’s expanding population centres, the region offers access to several important trade corridors.
The UAE’s established ports, airports, industrial zones and logistics infrastructure strengthen its appeal as a potential manufacturing and distribution centre.
Manufacturers operating from the country can potentially serve domestic demand while accessing regional and international markets through established transport networks.
However, geographical advantage alone is insufficient. Competitive industrial locations must also offer predictable regulations, reliable energy supplies, skilled workers, access to financing and efficient customs procedures.
The opportunity for the UAE lies in combining these advantages with an industrial strategy focused on higher-value production rather than competing exclusively on manufacturing costs.
As international businesses diversify their operations, countries capable of offering integrated manufacturing and logistics solutions could attract a greater share of future industrial investment.
Technology is changing the economics of manufacturing at remarkable speed.
Robotics, artificial intelligence, industrial sensors, machine learning and advanced data analytics are allowing factories to operate with greater precision, consistency and flexibility.
Production lines that once required extensive manual intervention can increasingly monitor equipment performance, detect defects and adjust operating conditions using real-time information.
Predictive maintenance systems can identify potential machinery failures before they interrupt production, while automated quality control can improve consistency and reduce material waste.
These developments are particularly relevant for economies seeking to expand manufacturing without relying primarily on large pools of inexpensive labour.
For the UAE, intelligent manufacturing offers an opportunity to develop competitive industrial capabilities in sectors where technological sophistication, product quality and reliability carry greater commercial value. Advanced robotics can support precision manufacturing, while additive manufacturing, commonly known as 3D printing, enables certain components to be produced with less material waste and shorter development cycles.
Countries capable of offering integrated manufacturing and logistics solutions could attract a greater share of future industrial investment.
Digital twins, which create virtual representations of physical equipment or production systems, can help manufacturers simulate operational changes before implementing them.
Together, these technologies are making factories more adaptable.
Instead of producing enormous quantities of identical products, manufacturers can increasingly accommodate smaller production runs, customised specifications and faster design changes.
This flexibility could prove particularly valuable in industries such as aerospace, medical equipment, automotive components and specialised engineering.
Yet automation does not eliminate the need for people. It changes the skills manufacturers require.
Industrial growth will depend increasingly on engineers, robotics specialists, software developers, technicians and professionals capable of managing complex production systems.
Developing this workforce will require closer collaboration between educational institutions, technical training providers and industrial employers.
The competitive advantage of tomorrow’s manufacturing centres may therefore depend as much on the quality of their technical talent as on the sophistication of their machinery.
Successful manufacturing economies rarely develop around isolated factories. Their strength comes from interconnected networks of suppliers, service providers, research institutions, logistics operators and specialised industrial businesses. For the UAE, building these relationships will be essential to creating an industrial sector capable of generating sustained economic value. A factory assembling sophisticated equipment may depend on hundreds of supporting activities, from component production and packaging to equipment maintenance, software integration and quality certification.
When these capabilities develop locally, manufacturers can reduce certain sourcing delays, improve coordination and create opportunities for smaller businesses to participate in industrial supply chains. This multiplier effect is one reason manufacturing remains important to economic diversification. Industrial investment can stimulate demand across transport, professional services, engineering, construction, technology and workforce development.
It can also support the emergence of specialised small and medium-sized enterprises that supply larger manufacturers with components, technical services and customised solutions.
Across the wider Gulf, industrial diversification programmes are similarly encouraging investment in sectors that can create economic value beyond traditional resource industries.
However, building a successful ecosystem requires more than attracting international manufacturers to establish facilities.
Domestic suppliers must be capable of meeting demanding technical standards, achieving internationally recognised certifications and delivering products consistently. Access to affordable industrial financing is another important consideration, particularly for smaller manufacturers investing in advanced equipment. Research and development also play a central role. Partnerships between universities, technology centres and industry can help translate scientific innovation into commercially viable products.
Equally important is creating demand for locally manufactured goods without compromising competitiveness. Industrial procurement, export development and supplier training can help emerging manufacturers establish a commercial foothold while building the capabilities needed to compete internationally. The ultimate objective is to move progressively from basic assembly towards activities involving greater technical expertise, intellectual property and product development.
Energy efficiency, sustainability, access to critical materials and the ability to adapt quickly to technological change will increasingly influence investment decisions. Manufacturers face growing pressure to reduce emissions, minimise waste and demonstrate greater transparency across their supply chains.
For energy-intensive industries, the availability, reliability and cost of electricity can determine whether an investment is commercially attractive.
The Middle East’s expanding clean energy capabilities could create opportunities for industrial operations seeking to improve their environmental performance, although the economics will differ across sectors.
Water efficiency will also remain important, particularly for manufacturing activities operating in arid environments. Circular manufacturing models, which emphasise recycling, material recovery and extending product lifecycles, could open additional commercial opportunities.

articles.title: UAE official emerges as late contender to lead UN - Financial Times
articles.summary: UAE official emerges as late contender to lead UN  Financial TimesEXCLUSIVE: Senior UAE diplomat Lana Nusseibeh enters race for UN chief  ReutersUAE's Lana Nusseibeh expected to enter candidate race for UN secretary-general  The Jerusalem PostUAE’s Lana Nusseibeh emerges as contender for UN secretary-general; Grynspan leads straw polls  i24NEWS[UN: Oct. 16] Editors’ Picks: SecGen Race Tightens, Refugee Agency Troubles & Lots More  PassBlue
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
A senior official from the United Arab Emirates is emerging as a contender to be the next secretary-general of the UN, electrifying the succession battle as it becomes mired in geopolitical infighting.
Supporters of Lana Nusseibeh have been sounding out missions at the UN, where she is well known as a former Emirati ambassador to the world body, to test the waters for her candidacy, diplomats say. UN insiders anticipate Nusseibeh, a minister of state at the UAE’s foreign ministry, could enter the race as early as this week.
The incumbent António Guterres is due to step down at the end of 2026, after two five-year terms overshadowed first by Covid and then by war. His successor will inherit an organisation in turmoil. The UN faces an acute budgetary crisis at a time when its authority on the world stage is at a historically low ebb and as the US, traditionally its biggest donor, is pushing for radical cuts.
After six months of public hustings at the UN and around the world, the three leading official candidates are still battling to win over all five of the permanent members of the UN Security Council (P5), each of whom can wield a veto on the choice of a successor.
The frontrunner Rebeca Grynspan, a former vice-president of Costa Rica and the head of the UN body on trade and development, last week won nine “encourage” votes in the latest Security Council straw poll. That would be enough in the final vote to secure the post, but she also had two “disapprovals” from veto-wielders.
The second-ranked candidate Rafael Grossi, the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency, also had two “disapprovals”.
The near deadlock is encouraging a fresh crop of candidates to consider throwing their hat into the ring at this late stage, according to people familiar with the state of the contest. The most high-profile — yet also, diplomats say, probably the most controversial — of the putative contenders is Nusseibeh.
She was a popular figure at the world body as the UAE’s UN ambassador from 2013 to 2024. For over a decade, the polished diplomat has articulated the UAE’s policies and defended its record at a time when it has been playing an increasingly assertive role in world affairs as both an investor and geopolitical actor.
The UAE has a close relationship with the Trump administration, but Nusseibeh could face a stiff challenge in distancing herself from the controversies over the UAE’s interventions in its region and beyond.
The UAE has faced intense criticism in particular over its role in Sudan, where it has backed the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces rebel group, which is accused of widespread atrocities in the country’s civil war. Abu Dhabi denies arming any of the warring factions.
A particular question hanging over her candidacy would be whether Saudi Arabia, the dominant Gulf power, would oppose it. Some regional analysts think it unlikely Riyadh would object to her candidacy, as the kingdom — under fire by Iran-backed Houthi rebels — attempts to mend a rift with Abu Dhabi over their disagreements in Yemen.
But Giorgio Cafiero, chief executive and founder of geopolitical risk consultancy Gulf State Analytics, said the prospect of an Emirati secretary-general “could raise concerns in Riyadh”.
The Gulf powerhouses “have a very competitive relationship, with divergent agendas across the broader region”, Cafiero said. “This is not to say that Saudi Arabia would necessarily actively oppose such a candidacy,” he added, but “the rivalry between the two countries tends to play out in a zero-sum manner.”
There was an informal understanding in the UN General Assembly this year that it was Latin America’s time to hold the post, and that a woman should take charge after nine male secretaries-general. But the US, which traditionally has the most influence on the decision, has started to play down in public the role of region and gender in the selection.
“We understand there is a desire for regional rotation,” Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, said after last week’s vote. “Of course if the best candidate’s a woman we would welcome that but we really just need the best candidate.”
“The Latin Americans are going to fight tooth and claw to have one of their own as secretary-general,” said Richard Gowan, a UN expert at the International Crisis Group. “But the veto powers may not care.”
Among other names circulating, UN diplomats say, is a former Turkish foreign minister, Feridun Sinirlioğlu, the head of the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe. There are also at least two more Latin American officials taking soundings.
Grynspan’s supporters stress she has won five out of the six votes so far, and is the only contender with a record of reform at the UN. Close observers of the UN say her two “disapprovals” are not insuperable and may reflect attempts by P5 countries to elicit concessions from her over appointments to jobs and her priorities. Such bargaining is a regular feature of UN succession races.
In 1996 Kofi Annan faced a P5 “disapproval” until the closing stages of the race, before he was ultimately appointed in part because the US saw him as an unflamboyant figure who would not rock the boat.
David Steven, a senior fellow at the UN Foundation, said the current “field” of candidates was “not yet dead” but that there was mounting expectation of new candidates joining the fray.
Among the scenarios, he said, was that if a new entrant failed to win support, a “UN safe pair of hands” could yet win the prize, not least given that the US insists on a candidate with a serious reform agenda.
“The Security Council should get on with it,” he said. “It is ridiculous that the 15 members should take this long. The candidate will end up with less time for the transition than the Security Council had to make its choice.”

articles.summary: 2 men rearrested in UK on suspicion of assisting Iran over suspected plot at a US-run air base  AP NewsTwo men rearrested on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence service in RAF Fairford incident  CNNTwo men rearrested in suspected plot on U.K. air base used by U.S. bombers  The Washington PostTwo men re-arrested on suspicion of assisting Iran intelligence after RAF Fairford incident  BBCUK police arrest pair on suspicion of helping Iranian intelligen...
articles.full_text:
LONDON (AP) — British police said Tuesday they have rearrested two men on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence service over a suspected plot at a U.S.-run air base in England last month.
Counter Terrorism Policing said the men, a 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old dual U.K.-Iranian national, were arrested under the National Security Act.
One of the suspects was first arrested on Sept. 27, when the suspected plot against the U.S.-run base at RAF Fairford took place. The air base in western England has been used to bomb Iran during this year’s war.
The second suspect was first arrested on Oct. 1. Until Tuesday the men had been bailed pending more investigation.
Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant — gasoline — in three vans at the site, but no explosives.
British authorities have linked Tehran to the incident, which led the U.S. to pull its bombers from RAF Fairford. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the apparent plot was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard, or IRGC.
Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.
Five other men in their 20s were arrested earlier then released on bail pending further investigation. No one has yet been charged.
Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the U.K., said detectives are looking at “many lines of enquiry involved in this hugely complex investigation.”
“This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement,” he said in a statement.
“Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it,” he added.
Last week the head of Britain’s MI5 spy agency warned that both Iran and Russia were expanding their attacks against the U.K., and that the RAF base incident was not unique.
Ken McCallum, who leads the U.K.’s domestic security service, said Tehran is seeking to intensify its attacks in Britain beyond the traditional targets of Iranians opposed to the country’s Islamic authorities.
In all, more than 50 people have been arrested over Iran-linked plots in the past year, McCallum said.

Moroccan Prime Minister Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri reaffirmed Rabat’s support for a peaceful resolution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict based on a two-state solution during an address to parliament on Monday, outlining her government’s five-year program.
Mansouri reiterated Morocco’s “long-standing position on the Palestinian cause and Jerusalem” and its “support for a peaceful settlement based on a two-state solution that would ensure a just and lasting peace.”
Israel and Morocco re-established diplomatic ties in 2020 as part of the Abraham Accords, with Morocco among the first countries to normalize relations with Israel under the agreements. In September, the two countries announced plans to open embassies and appoint ambassadors, further strengthening bilateral ties.
Morocco’s first female prime minister outlined a government agenda focused on tackling corruption, strengthening social welfare, integrating young people into the economy, protecting national sovereignty and building a more productive economy.
Pressure to address unemployment, economic issues
The government faces pressure to address youth grievances over employment, education and healthcare, which contributed to the Gen Z protests in 2025. Youth unemployment and limited economic opportunities have also featured prominently in debates surrounding migration from Morocco, including the mass crossing into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in July.
Mansouri pledged to strengthen mechanisms for tackling anti-competitive practices and introduce new procedures to scrutinize public contracts and investigate collusion. Companies awarded public contracts will also be legally required to allocate 30% of their contract value to Moroccan small and medium-sized enterprises, she said.
To address the rising cost of living, Mansouri outlined a strategy focused on tackling the causes of price increases, expanding social protection and improving public services. The government plans to introduce automatic social assistance for eligible households equivalent to their monthly electricity bills, capped at MAD 100 for their primary residence.
The government will also gradually reform income tax to increase workers’ take-home pay and encourage formal employment.

They expressed their mutual commitment to continuing a regular trust-based political dialogue and building up interaction in the trade, economic, investment, cultural and humanitarian areas. The parties have reaffirmed the demand for continued effective cooperation between Russia and Saudi Arabia in the OPEC+ format.
The ministers considered current topics on the international and Middle East agendas, including the situation in the Persian Gulf area. They expressed their concern over the tension in the south of the Arabian Peninsula and in the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait. Both sides stated the importance of ensuring the safety of navigation and unhindered passage of ships through all international waterways.
The Russia-Saudi partnership is becoming a central pillar of the wider BRICS + Middle Eastern-Eurasian integrated economic ecosystem and an anchor of what analysts increasingly describe as greater Eurasian-Middle Eastern comprehensive integration, a process that is destined to reshape global supply chains, investment flows, effective connectivity projects, and industrial cooperation patterns across the Global South.
As Riyadh accelerates its transport and port modernization, Saudi participation in the INSTC becomes not only feasible but strategically advantageous. Linking the Kingdom to Russia–India–Central Asia trade corridors would strengthen Saudi Arabia’s vision of becoming the premier logistics gateway of the Middle East. Saudi inclusion in the INSTC and potential integration into the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) within a trade deal format would dovetail perfectly with Vision 2030’s logistics pillar, creating a multimodal link between the Red Sea, the Gulf Cooperation Council and Russia’s northern routes. Such a move would elevate Saudi Arabia from a regional shipping leader to a critical node in Eurasia’s emerging transport architecture and global free trade promotion.
Key pillars of Russian–Saudi cooperation now span energy, agriculture, and advanced technology, reflecting a rapidly diversifying partnership. From refined petroleum to wheat and meat, Saudi imports are rising sharply as Russia’s agricultural exports to the Kingdom surge to historic levels. From sunflower oil shipments totaling 88,000 tonnes to a fivefold surge in soybean oil exports, Russia is strengthening its role in Saudi Arabia’s food supply chain. Meat exports have jumped nearly sevenfold, and even finished goods like coffee extracts and grain-processed products have grown 20-fold, revealing a broadening agro-industrial bridge.
Riyadh has become a key market for Russian poultry and beef, up sevenfold in five years. Russia’s agricultural exports to Saudi Arabia are on track to surpass US$1.4 billion by 2030, with grain anchoring this fast-growing trade corridor. Yet the real momentum lies in rising shipments of meat, processed foods, and vegetable oils, sectors poised for exceptional expansion. This performance is not accidental. Over the past decade, the two sides have implemented more than 40 joint investment projects in ICT, petrochemicals, transport, infrastructure, and cyber-technology. Russian investment in Saudi Arabia increased sixfold in 2024, while Saudi investments in Russia rose by 11% over the same period.
The collaboration between the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) and Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) remains a symbol of this new synergy. Their joint US$10-billion investment platform, as well as recent agreements such as PIF’s investment in the Russian logistics operator PLT (one of Russia’s top five logistics operators) and its US$100-million commitment to the Russia’s largest technological park—the Tushino Technopark – demonstrate mutual strategic trust and a shared desire to develop complementary value chains. In a complimentary relationship, Russia is also interested in cooperating with Riyadh’s Techno Valley, a key strategic project for Saudi Arabia, focused on the development of applied research and the commercialization of technologies in priority areas, including the chemical industry and new materials, developments in biology, ecology, agriculture, and telecommunications.
There is clear recognition that the industrial cooperation between Russia and Saudi Arabia is entering a qualitatively new stage. These include:
Machine-Building & Robotics
Russia’s national project for the development of machine tool production, industrial automation, and robotics presents significant opportunities for joint ventures with Saudi industrial clusters. As Saudi Arabia seeks to become a manufacturing hub under Vision 2030, the localization of Russian industrial technologies, some of the world’s most cost-efficient and resilient, could give the Kingdom a decisive competitive edge.
Shipbuilding & Metallurgy
Cooperation in shipbuilding and metallurgy, two traditional strongholds of Russian engineering, aligns with Saudi Arabia’s ambitions to expand its role as a global maritime logistics hub for the Red Sea, Arabian Gulf, and Indian Ocean regions. Joint shipyard projects in the Middle East would represent a breakthrough in Eurasian industrial integration.
Aerospace & Aviation
Russia’s fully import-substituted MC-21 and SJ-100 aircraft are emerging as potential export products for the burgeoning Saudi aviation market, which is projected to reach US$11.92 billion by 2033. With Saudi carriers planning to order more than 100 new aircraft in the next five years, and Flyadeal expanding its fleet to 100 jets by 2030, Russia has a real opportunity to offer cost-efficient alternatives to Western manufacturers. Additionally, the light aircraft LMS-901 Baikal, slated for delivery in 2026, could fit perfectly into Saudi Arabia’s regional connectivity programs.
Mining, Rare Earths, and Strategic Minerals
In one of the most strategically important developments, Riyadh has expressed interest in cooperating with Russia in the exploration and processing of rare earth metals, a sector dominated by a handful of countries and vital for global high-tech production. Saudi Arabia recently increased its estimated mineral wealth to US$1.5 trillion, including substantial rare earth reserves. Russian expertise in ore beneficiation, mining equipment, separation technologies, and metallurgical engineering positions Moscow as a natural partner. Beyond rare earths, Russia offers advanced solutions for the mining of titanium, aluminum, and other high-value materials, all of which are crucial for the aerospace, automotive, and defense industries globally.
Agriculture and Food Security
Agricultural cooperation is becoming one of the fastest-growing segments of bilateral trade. Having already detailed the rapid growth in food trade, it bears repeating that agriculture stands as a major future driver of Russian–Saudi economic ties. Its breadth from basic commodities to high-value processed goods offers unmatched long-term potential. Russia’s agricultural exports to Saudi Arabia are projected to exceed US$1.4 billion by 2030. These trends illustrate how Russia is becoming one of the Kingdom’s key partners in food security, a central pillar of Vision 2030. Russian agro-based companies must seize the full potential of this growth.

Saudi Arabia’s digital market is opening up to Russia’s next-generation tech enterprises, from AI-driven logistics to cybersecurity solutions. This engagement reinforces the broader Russia–Saudi strategy of forging cutting-edge industrial and technological partnerships. It offers Saudi partners a detailed view of Russian competencies in cybersecurity systems, hybrid logistics, fintech platforms for international settlements, electric mobility, smart city technologies, digital construction platforms, aerospace drones and surveying systems, water and air purification, and industrial robotics. Companies such as Hyper, Geoscan, Ecothermics, NexTouch, Aerolife, RealPay, and major players like Sberbank, Sistema, and the Russian-Arab Business Council showcase export-ready solutions designed for the Saudi market. This high-tech component is particularly important as the Kingdom accelerates its digital transformation and seeks partners not dependent on Western regulatory systems.

Sateyndra Pathak
DOHA
Qatar is preparing to announce a new regional defence partnership to strengthen air defence, counter-drone capabilities and cybersecurity, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of State for Defence Affairs HE Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman bin Hassan Al Thani said on Monday, warning that the global economic impact of disruptions to energy supplies had yet to reach its peak.
Speaking during a fireside chat with CNN national security analyst Peter Bergen at the eighth Global Security Forum 2026 in Doha, Sheikh Saoud highlighted Qatar’s longstanding defence cooperation with the United States and international allies, while stressing the need for stronger regional partnerships amid evolving security threats.
“We haven’t reached the peak with respect to energy,” he said, warning that further repercussions could emerge “in the coming days and months”.
Sheikh Saoud said disruptions to energy supplies from Qatar and the wider Gulf could drive up costs worldwide, affect trade between East and West, and put pressure on overseas investments and international development assistance. He cautioned against imposing transit fees on vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz, saying the resulting uncertainty would ultimately affect consumers globally.
On defence cooperation, Sheikh Saoud highlighted Qatar’s partnership with Washington, saying more than 90 percent of attacks had been prevented through shared expertise and military capabilities developed over the past three to four decades.
He described Al Udeid Air Base as a Qatari military facility hosting US forces and personnel from other partner countries for training, exercises, humanitarian missions and regional operations. Qatar continues to develop the base to meet the operational needs of its armed forces and support joint activities with allies.
Sheikh Saoud said Qatar was strengthening its domestic defence capabilities and working with regional partners and international allies to address emerging threats. He stressed that diplomatic engagement and mediation must go hand in hand with military preparedness.
“Mediation doesn’t mean that we should not be ready for any defensive action from our side,” he said.
Addressing relations with Iran, Sheikh Saoud said Qatar had maintained communication with Tehran despite regional conflict and bilateral differences. He expressed hope that mediation efforts involving Qatar, Pakistan and Oman would help secure an agreement between the United States, Iran and other parties.

US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate
The US State Department has ordered some diplomats and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as attacks escalate, with three people killed in strikes across the country.
Saudi authorities said debris from a drone intercepted during an attempted attack on an oil field killed two people, while one person died after a strike at the King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
Conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia has been rising in the past month.
The Houthis have responded to Saudi strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in Saudi Arabia. A recent strike on Riyadh's international airport was the deadliest in the kingdom in years.
"The US Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia," a state department spokesperson said in a statement.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," it added.
The spokesperson also warned "the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly".
In the latest attack on the King Fahd International Airport eight people sustained injuries that ranged from "minor to serious", officials said.
No details of the attack have yet been given, but the strike comes after airports in Saudi Arabia have been repeatedly targeted by Houthi forces.
The energy ministry has also not said who had launched the drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field near the border with the United Arab Emirates that left two people injured.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. Conflicts escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led military coalition tried to restore the government's rule.
An informal ceasefire had been in place for the past four years, but it unravelled in July after the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The group's "maritime embargo" in the Bab al-Mandab Strait along Yemen's south-western coast has contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

articles.title: New Mexico sues Epstein's lawyer, accountant over trafficking cover-up
articles.summary: New Mexico's attorney general sued Jeffrey Epstein's lawyer and accountant Wednesday, accusing them of helping conceal the disgraced financier's sex trafficking operation at his sp...
articles.full_text:
New Mexico's attorney general sued Jeffrey Epstein's lawyer and accountant Wednesday, accusing them of helping conceal the disgraced financier's sex trafficking operation at his sprawling ranch in the state.
The lawsuit seeks to stop attorney Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn from accepting any payments from Epstein's estate, estimated at more than $100 million.
Indyke worked as Epstein’s attorney for roughly two decades. Both he and Kahn have testified in Congress that they did not know about Epstein’s abuse, though New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez has a different view.
He said Indyke and Kahn "stand to benefit substantially” from Epstein's estate unless a court intervenes.
"Those resources rightfully belong in the hands of survivors,” Torrez said, referring to victims of Epstein’s abuse.
Epstein killed himself in August 2019 in a federal jail in New York City, where he was awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges.
Epstein’s former girlfriend and close associate, Ghislaine Maxwell, is serving a 20-year prison sentence after her 2021 conviction on sex trafficking charges in New York. Witness testimony at Maxwell’s trial alleged she and Epstein had sexually abused women at the New Mexico ranch.
Epstein purchased the ranch in Stanley, New Mexico, a sparsely populated ranching community about 30 miles (48 kilometers) south of Santa Fe, in 1993. He built a 26,700-square-foot mansion with a sprawling courtyard, a living room roughly the size of the average American home, and a private airstrip and helipad.
Epstein never faced charges in New Mexico, though the state attorney general's office in 2019 confirmed that it was investigating and planned to forward its findings to federal authorities in New York. Hector Balderas, who was attorney general at the time, said the state’s outdated laws failed to protect children from abuse.
Torrez reopened the state’s investigation this year. In August, he sued the Department of Justice, accusing it of blocking the state from investigating alleged sex crimes at the ranch. The lawsuit said state prosecutors faced "sustained resistance” to the kind of information-sharing common between state and federal investigators. The Justice Department said it was not releasing some information the state requested to avoid disclosing victim-identifying information.
Also in August, a commission established by state lawmakers to investigate the allegations and whether local authorities looked the other way released a 119-page report that found that authorities repeatedly deferred to investigations in New York, Palm Beach, Florida, and the Virgin Islands, while leaving Epstein’s offenses in New Mexico unexamined and unpunished.
The ranch was sold by Epstein’s estate in 2023 - with proceeds going toward creditors - to the family of Don Huffines, a Republican recently appointed Texas’ state comptroller.

articles.title: French students turn awkward slogan into protest rallying cry
articles.summary: A nonsensical phrase, allegedly used by undercover police attempting to mimic immigrant youth slang online, has become a viral symbol of France's ongoing student demonstrations. Hu...
articles.full_text:
A nonsensical phrase, allegedly used by undercover police attempting to mimic immigrant youth slang online, has become a viral symbol of France's ongoing student demonstrations.
Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators have flooded France's streets to support student protesters, armed with a rallying cry that translates to almost nothing.
The phrase "Bismillah, c'est les ténèbres" roughly translates to "In the name of God, it's the darkness" – a mash-up of the Arabic expression "bismillah," which French youth colloquially use like "let's go," and a gloomy French idiom for a hopeless situation.
The slogan originated in early October when high school students organizing school blockades on Snapchat spotted a suspected infiltrator. A user named "Mamadou" asked to join a private group, messaging: "Hi, in the name of God, it's the darkness. When's the blockade, wallah, bro?"
The New York Times reported the message was sent repeatedly under different profiles – including Mamadou and Abdellah – with Algerian flag emojis. Students suspected the sender was a police officer posing as a teenager.
While French authorities have not commented, the French TV program "Quotidien" reported police in Aix-en-Provence used the phrase on Snapchat to pose as students.
Viewing the wording as an absurd caricature of immigrant youth slang, protesters embraced it as evidence of how out of touch and quick to profile the authorities seemed.
The phrase quickly spread to marches across France – from Place de la Bastille in Paris to Toulouse, Lille and Clermont-Ferrand – spawning merchandise and parody videos before jumping to protests in Belgium and Italy.
The student movement began in September over crowded classrooms and teacher shortages, later expanding to protest the high cost of living. Turnout peaked the weekend of Oct. 17 with hundreds of thousands in the streets. On Oct. 13, the Interior Ministry estimated 161,500 demonstrators, while student organizers claimed 480,000.
Youssef el Chazli, a sociologist at Paris 8 University, told Al Jazeera the slogan "reinforces an image of out-of-touch policemen filled with stereotypes" that disproportionately target youths of Arab and African descent. He added that protest creativity "will draw heavily on youths' subcultures."
The unrest has also sparked political backlash. France's far right blamed Muslim youths for the violence, while former President Donald Trump claimed the demonstrations were about "Islam wanting to take over."

articles.title: UN warns world on course for 2.6 C warming this century
articles.summary: Current global commitments to cut greenhouse gas emissions fall far short of Paris Agreement goals, putting the world on track for 2.6 degrees Celsius of warming this century, the...
articles.full_text:
Current global commitments to cut greenhouse gas emissions fall far short of Paris Agreement goals, putting the world on track for 2.6 degrees Celsius of warming this century, the U.N. warned Wednesday.
The report by the U.N. Environment Programme (UNEP) highlights the gap between rhetoric and action on global warming and the challenge facing political leaders at November's COP31 climate summit.
Even if countries deliver their latest climate pledges in full, global temperatures could still rise 2.6 C above preindustrial levels by 2100, the annual Emissions Gap Report said.
That would blow past the historic goal agreed to in Paris: keeping warming well below 2 C while striving for a safer 1.5 C. Any chance of meeting the 1.5 C target had been "lost" due to decades of insufficient climate action, the report said.
"The world can no longer avoid overshooting the 1.5-C limit, and the consequences are already devastating," U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a statement launching the closely watched report.
"Deadly floods, brutal heatwaves, raging wildfires, lost lives, crippled economies, deepening inequalities, and those least responsible are suffering first and worst," he added.
Overall, global greenhouse gas emissions in 2025 were broadly on par with record levels in 2024. The difference between the two years was insignificant, the report said.
Carbon emissions from burning coal, oil and gas – the main driver of climate change – rose slightly in 2025 compared to the previous year.
Guterres said deep, immediate cuts were needed to protect humanity from worsening impacts, but instead, emissions remain at record levels, and national climate plans and current policies fall dangerously short.
Sticking with current policies would result in warming hitting 2.8 C, the report said.
Scientists warn that every additional fraction of a degree Celsius above 1.5 C increases extreme weather events and the likelihood of irreversible changes to the planet, from dying coral reefs to melting permafrost.
The world has already warmed roughly 1.4 C relative to preindustrial times, and crossing 1.5 C is expected in a matter of years.
The G-20 accounts for three-fourths of global emissions, but Guterres said "all countries, especially the big emitters, must do more" to stop heating the planet.
This latest UNEP warming outlook is worse than last year's due to the formal withdrawal of the U.S. from the Paris accord and upward revisions of historical emissions, report co-author Anne Olhoff said.
Emissions growth slowed among the G-20, but the U.S. was a "major exception," the report added.
Among the world's top-six emitters, preliminary data for 2025 showed emissions increases in the U.S., Indonesia and China and decreases in India, Russia and the European Union.
But in terms of magnitude, the U.S. increase of 133 megatons of carbon dioxide equivalent "far exceeded" that of any other country, driven by higher electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation.
The next-largest increase was recorded in Turkey, which is hosting the U.N. climate summit in Antalya from Nov. 9-20.
The U.S. is the world's second-largest polluter, behind China. President Donald Trump has called climate change a hoax and rolled back clean energy policies while boosting fossil fuel production.
UNEP Executive Secretary Inger Andersen told reporters that no country was shielded from climate change, and impacts were being felt "on every nation on the planet, including the U.S."
The report details a scenario with a 50% chance of bringing global warming back down to 1.5 C by 2100.
To get there, warming must peak around 1.8 C by 2050, and vast amounts of CO2 would have to be removed from the atmosphere to bring temperatures down further.
But this scenario assumes immediate emissions cuts of 6% annually until 2035 – nowhere near current projections.
"The main takeaway is simple – governments need to get on with enacting policies that cut fossil fuel use as soon as possible," Bill Hare, CEO of global policy institute Climate Analytics, said.
Some climate-vulnerable developing nations have accused bigger emitters of abandoning the Paris goals, and a showdown over the 1.5 C target is expected at COP31.
"This is a historic failure of political leadership. The science has been clear for decades, but governments have chosen delay over action. The consequences will be measured in lives lost, not just degrees of warming," Mohamed Adow, director of Kenya-based think tank Power Shift Africa, said.
Guterres agreed there was a climate "leadership gap" but said overshooting 1.5 C "is not surrender."

articles.title: Thousands march in Greece in France-inspired student protests
articles.summary: Thousands of Greek students protested nationwide Wednesday against the high cost of living, citing grievances similar to those fueling recent demonstrations in France and across Eu...
articles.full_text:
Thousands of Greek students protested nationwide Wednesday against the high cost of living, citing grievances similar to those fueling recent demonstrations in France and across Europe.
“In Greece, like in France, we are demanding public, free education,” said Katia Koubousidou, head of a student union at Aristotle University of Thessaloniki.
“This will not be a one-off protest. We have a plan to continue our demonstrations.”
Police estimated at least 5,000 people attended the Athens protest. Similar protests also occurred in other major Greek cities.
Dozens of students earlier Tuesday set up tents on Athens' Syntagma Square, facing Parliament and on a pedestrian street in Thessaloniki. State hospital doctors and civil servants also went on strike Wednesday.
Secondary school pupils and teachers are protesting poor infrastructure, a shortage of staff and insufficient public spending on education.
The conservative Greek government has sought in recent days to avoid any parallel with the protests and violence in France.
Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said Monday that the country would "never return to the era of great social unrest" during the financial crisis more than a decade ago, marked by unpopular austerity measures.
French cities experienced some of the country's worst rioting in recent years Saturday, with public buildings torched, hundreds of shops looted and more than 2,000 people arrested.
According to EU data agency Eurostat, Greece in 2023 spent 3.3% of national output on education, among the lowest share in the bloc and far below the European average of 4.7%.
“Authorities do not want (people to have) quality education, so we don't understand what is going on," said Maria, a 57-year-old municipal worker at the Athens protest.
Greek education unions and student groups have long called for additional spending on dilapidated buildings and more staff.
“School buildings are terrible and poorly maintained,” said Yiannis Papanikolaou, a 17-year-old school pupil from the Athens district of Exarchia.
“Falling plaster, broken windows, faulty radiators,” he said.
“I think something might change because of what France is doing. France will spur Greece,” he said.
Teachers' union OLME said there is a shortage of 15,000 secondary school teachers nationwide.
Earlier this month, falling roof plaster injured a 14-year-old schoolboy in a classroom in Thermi, near the city of Thessaloniki in northern Greece.
A similar incident occurred Monday at the entrance of an Athens school, outside operating hours. A major school complex in Athens has been closed for almost two weeks over a gas leak scare under investigation, affecting some 4,000 pupils.

A Mirage 2000D fighter jet crashed in eastern France while returning from a mission late Tuesday, killing at least one person, the Armed Forces Ministry said Wednesday.
The crew consisted of a fighter pilot and a weapons systems officer from the French Air and Space Force. One body has been recovered and a search for the second crew member is ongoing.
The plane went down at 9 p.m. GMT Tuesday near the town of Rogeville, about 18 kilometers (11 miles) northwest of the city of Nancy. Local prefect Yves Seguy told reporters that a wooded area where the plane crashed was searched overnight in adverse weather.
"It appears that at least one of the crew members was not able to eject," an air force spokesperson Col. David Papalardo, told franceinfo radio.
An investigation into the cause of the crash has been opened.
The plane was attached to the nearby 133 Nancy-Ochey air base. Col. Ludovic Humbert, the base commandant, said the weapons systems officer was a seasoned soldier who was teaming up with a young pilot. The plane had begun its final approach as it returned to base from a night training mission when the crash happened.
The Mirage 2000D specializes in ground-attack missions. A two-seat aircraft, it is designed to operate in complex environments, the ministry said. It supports conventional air operations and power-projection missions.

articles.title: Australia lawmaker's legs amputated after 'targeted' car attack
articles.summary: Australian lawmaker Helen Haines underwent a double leg amputation after being struck by a car in what police described as a targeted attack, her husband said Wednesday, calling he...
articles.full_text:
Australian lawmaker Helen Haines underwent a double leg amputation after being struck by a car in what police described as a targeted attack, her husband said Wednesday, calling her a "fighter."
Haines is in stable condition at a Melbourne hospital after being struck Monday near her office in Wangaratta, about 200 kilometers (124.27 miles) northeast of the state capital.
The incident prompted soul-searching in a country where political violence is rare, but police have documented a steady rise in threats and abuse against elected officials in recent years.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese led tributes to Haines, an independent member of parliament and a passionate campaigner for transparency and against corruption.
He acknowledged the need for Australians to turn down the temperature and embrace respectful disagreement over polarization.
Speaking at the hospital Wednesday, Haines' husband Phil, married almost 40 years, said after days in intensive care, surgeons amputated both her legs.
"But the good news in all this is Helen is alive and she's stable. That is the most important thing for our family," he said.
"The two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind."
"Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person."
"Helen's road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter."
The man alleged to have wounded Haines in what police called a targeted attack faced court for the first time Wednesday.
Brendan Nugent, 43, was charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury and intentionally causing serious injury, as well as the federal crime of harming a public official, which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison.
He also was charged with cultivating a cannabis plant and possession of the drug, according to court documents. Nugent appeared at a courthouse in Wangaratta.
He did not speak in court or apply for bail, and his next hearing is scheduled for Feb. 4.
Governor-General Sam Mostyn, King Charles III's official representative in Australia, said the nation was crying out for decency.
"Australians are yearning for kindness and care, and they're asking us why we've lost the great skill of disagreeing well," Mostyn said alongside Haines's husband Phil.
The motive remains unknown, and authorities will not speculate while the investigation is ongoing.
But police said Wednesday they were examining all possible leads, including that Nugent may have held radical anti-government views.
"We're examining social media associations, talking to witnesses, friends and colleagues," Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush told journalists.
Bush said authorities had no intelligence on the suspect and had seen nothing to suggest he posed an immediate threat.
Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett pointed to a growing and concerning level of extremist views online.

articles.title: Putin welcomes Witkoff with fresh Ukraine peace talks in offing
articles.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin hosted U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff Wednesday to discuss new proposals for ending the war in Ukraine, amid Washington's latest push to stop Eur...
articles.full_text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin hosted U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff Wednesday to discuss new proposals for ending the war in Ukraine, amid Washington's latest push to stop Europe's bloodiest conflict since World War II.
The talks in St. Petersburg, Witkoff's ninth meeting with Putin, included a goodwill gesture from Russia: the release of a retired U.S. schoolteacher held in Russia.
The encounter prompted concerns in Kyiv and among its allies that the United States is backing away from Ukraine, at times holding back real-time intelligence on Russian attacks and hobbling Ukraine's military communications.
The latest talks came more than two years after President Donald Trump promised in his election campaign to end the Ukraine war within 24 hours.
Witkoff flew into St. Petersburg Wednesday morning, a day after conducting what a U.S. official called "constructive" talks in Oslo with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the leaders of Finland and Norway, and European and NATO representatives. President Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to end the war or face "a very bad thing."
U.S.-Ukraine ties have deteriorated sharply since Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier this month, which he said would help lower prices in the United States.
Since the diesel deal, Ukraine has complained of disruption to some intelligence sharing and to its use of the Starlink military satellite system, though Zelenskyy said Tuesday's Oslo meeting had reached an agreement to resolve those issues.
Citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that billionaire Elon Musk ordered last week the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on to track Russian ballistic missile strikes.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Musk has said any such decision is made by the U.S. military or the president. Trump has said he was not responsible. U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth signaled Tuesday that the problem lay in the terms of service Kyiv needed to comply with.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that Witkoff's meeting with Zelenskyy was positive and that Witkoff would share the results with Russia. He also reiterated that Washington had not pulled back Kyiv's ability to access Starlink.
"He will now, armed with those ideas, be able to go to St. Petersburg and share them with the Russian side, and let's see if we can make some progress," he said.
Despite the apparently cordial nature of Tuesday's meeting in Oslo, Trump, in comments Tuesday at the White House, remained frustrated with Zelenskyy, whom he has repeatedly rebuked and suggested should be replaced.
"He's going to have to want to make a deal, because I don't think his people are going to stand for it any longer," Trump told reporters on the eve of the talks in Russia.
Putin, who has shown few signs of compromising on his central war aims – which include full Russian control of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine and no NATO membership for Kyiv – received Witkoff in the Constantine Palace, an imperial edifice in his home city.
Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's special investment envoy and his key liaison for potential economic and financial deals with the U.S., also attended the meeting with Witkoff, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said.
A U.S. official said Ukraine brought new ideas and proposals to the Oslo talks, which made "meaningful progress" toward a coordinated approach to engaging with Russia.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the talks covered "key elements of a comprehensive peace framework," including security guarantees for Ukraine, a postwar economic plan and a broader European security architecture.
Witkoff aimed to "create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations," the official said. Zelenskyy said he hoped to discuss key issues on how to end the war during a trilateral meeting with Putin and Trump.
The Kremlin has repeatedly said that any Putin-Zelenskyy meeting would need to be painstakingly prepared by aides to make it worthwhile and that much legwork would be required for an overall agreement.
Trump said Tuesday he raised the idea with Putin of freeing Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired U.S. schoolteacher being held in Russia on mercenary charges he denies.
Putin told Witkoff that Hubbard was at the airport waiting to fly back to the U.S. with him. Witkoff thanked Putin for the goodwill gesture.
Hubbard was first detained in April 2022 and later sentenced to six years and 10 months on charges whose veracity his family and U.S.-based lawyer question.
